#3348. Where to find the Port Gellhorn serial killer in GTA 6

Three missing person cases can only mean one thing...

Three missing person cases can only mean one thing...

Finding Port Gelhorn's missing tourists and the serial killer in Grand Theft Auto 6 takes you on a twisted journey around the town, one with few guideposts and a lot of chances to get stuck. It's a macabre scavenger hunt with only a few pictures and knowledge of the surrounding area to go by, though the reward at the end is comparatively small. This is a quest where the storytelling, more than anything else, is the reward.

Below, we explain where to find Gelhorn's missing tourists in GTA 6 and complete the serial killer side mission.

You'll first come across this exploration mission in the Starlet Motel office after Chapter 2 starts. Lucia can examine a set of missing persons posters on the wall next to Linda's desk. There's a tip line with a number to call, but it just takes you to a voice mailbox.

And that's the only hint to go off of, as the poster info gives you no clues and nowhere to look. There might be other clues hidden somewhere around town, but we didn't find them. Instead, we stumbled across the quest's starting location by accident. It's an old bunker-like warehouse across the street from Moses' garage, next to the scooter store. You can approach the front for a prompt to open the door, but it won't work. Walk down the right side of the warehouse, and look for a hole at the base. Crawl inside.

Despite how creepy the location is, there's nothing inside to harm you, though there is a jump scare midway through. Enter the red room and the trophy room beyond it, and interact with the photos there. You'll see locations showing each of the missing tourists, and these photos are stored in your phone gallery if you want to view them later. The quest prompt changes in the map menu, too, with a new prompt for each photo.

You can track them in any order. We're just listing them in the order we found them. We recommend tackling this part of the quest during the day, just so it's easier to make out landmarks.

The junkyard is where you'll find Susanne Keeble, and it's next to the Pay 'n' Spray shop in central Gelhorn. You're looking for a pink car, and if you're having trouble finding it, activate focus mode. The car will stand out as the only interactable object in the area. Report the body to the tip line after you find it.

Donald Miller's body is out at Wild Hog Point, the marshes outside Port Gelhorn. Head toward the tree with no leaves near the center of the marsh, and look in the water nearby to find a car. Interact with it, report the body, and move on. Someone picks up the line this time.

Patrick Murray is the final tourist, and his body is in a trailer at the far north end of Port Gelhorn in an abandoned trailer park near a water tower. The trailer in question is the blue one. Head inside, and pull up the floorboards near the door to discover Murray's body. The clipping in the trophy room mentioned a reward for information about him, though, for reasons you'll soon discover, the tip line operator isn't ready to pay out.

The tip line man asks you to return to the warehouse after finding the third body, and the quest can change depending on whether you go alone or with your partner. We played as Jason and went with Lucia, though who takes the lead doesn't matter. Your partner stays outside, and tense events unfold inside, after which the culprit dies and the quest ends. You can grab the killer's glasses as a unique "found" accessory for Jason if you want.

#3344. Markiplier’s Iron Lung Officially Returns In 3 Weeks With Exciting New Horror Release

Markiplier's Iron Lung is about to terrorize viewers once again.

Based on David Szymanski's hit viral video game of the same name, the horror film centers on Simon, a convict living in a distant future in which all stars, inhabited planets and most of humanity have vanished, and is tasked with exploring a desolate moon with an ocean of blood in a small submarine. Written, directed by and starring Markiplier, Iron Lung left critics somewhat divided but was a thorough smash with audiences and at the box office.

Now, nearly a year after the film hit theaters, Markiplier has offered a new update on his Iron Lung adaptation, revealing that it is officially getting a DVD and Blu-ray release. The horror hit, which is currently available for pre-order in both of its versions, is slated to release in three weeks, with the filmmaker indicating it will arrive around December 13, when he will also host a special livestream offering a complete behind-the-scenes look at the creation of the film and its unanswered questions.

In addition to the film itself, the Iron Lung Blu-ray and DVDs, which cost $30 and $20 respectively, are said to come with over three hours of never-before-seen bonus content, including a behind-the-scenes documentary entitled One with the Blood running just over two hours long, as well as various other featurettes and yet-to-be-announced content.

The long wait for an Iron Lung physical release is sure to have been a surprising one compared to the general three-to-four-month turnaround for other films. However, as Markiplier explains in the video above, the reason for this stemmed from a desire to prevent losing creative control over his hit movie, and the desire to give an in-depth Blu-ray experience.

It certainly falls in line with the way the filmmaker treated Iron Lung throughout its initial development, which was in and of itself a slow-but-steady process. After being announced in Spring 2023, production was hit with a few notable setbacks, including the 2023 SAG-AFTRA strike, as well as dealing with minor injuries from the fake blood used on set, which set a new world record with over 80,000 gallons used. Moreover, the film took nearly two years from when he finished its post-production to ultimately giving it a grassroots-like independent theatrical release.

Ultimately, Markiplier's efforts have frequently proven worthwhile for Iron Lung. Despite coming out in January, an infamously lackluster window at the box office, the movie saw its opening weekend projections continually increase as anticipation grew around it, with it ultimately opening to $18.2 million, well surpassing its production budget, which the filmmaker has estimated being between $4–5 million. By the end of its run, it had grossed $51.2 million, somewhere between 10-13 times its budget.

While not as talked-about as its successors, Markiplier's Iron Lung notably kicked off 2026 as the year of YouTubers-turned-filmmakers taking over the box office. The combined might of Curry Barker's Obsession and Kane Parsons' Backrooms, which together grossed close to $925 million, has seen Hollywood now turning to other similar stories and projects, while also pushing forward with new titles from both Barker and Parsons.

Obsession has become the latest in a long line of horror films made by YouTube creators, and it's just one of six films that shows their creativity.

Now that Iron Lung is slated for a physical media release, it will be interesting to see how much its previous success carries over into a medium that many studios have started to phase out. Considering the passionate fanbase Markiplier and the film have, and it being a limited-run release, there's a very real chance it could enjoy a similar level of success and, depending on the speed of its inventory sales, may even get a restocking at some point in the future.

Iron Lung is a film set in a post-apocalyptic future where a convict is tasked with exploring a blood ocean on a desolate moon. Utilizing a small submarine called the Iron Lung, he navigates the aftermath of the Quiet Rapture, which caused the disappearance of stars and habitable planets.

#3342. Legendary Critical Role Cast Members Officially Return With a Star-Studded New Guest Cast

Aabria Iyengar and Travis Willingham return in Campaign 4

It’s hard to believe the entire Critical Role table for Campaign 4 hasn’t been together since the Convergence arc in June. Since then, the Soldiers, Seekers, and Schemers tables have remained separate. Or, more accurately, the Seekers and Schemers tables have remained separate.

Since Critical Role Campaign 4 episode 31, "Trick of the Light," Critters haven’t seen hide nor hair of everyone’s favorite orc Druid, Thaisha Lloy. Nor have they received any confirmation about when, exactly, Travis Willingham will return with a new character, after his Paladin, Teor Pridesire, met an unfortunate end in episode 30, "Here in the Dark."

Luckily, the wait is finally over. Critical Role announced on Nov. 23 that its eagerly anticipated Soldiers table, featuring Aabria Iyengar as Thaisha, will return on Dec. 3 and Dec. 10 for a two-part Soldiers table arc. And she won’t be alone.

When the three tables split off in June last year, it seemed that the Soldiers table would consist only of Thaisha. In an interview with Polygon, Iyengar confirmed she wasn't sure at the time whether Thaisha’s story would be told through cold openings or off-camera. Later, however, the Critical Role team decided to give the Soldiers table a mini-arc following Thaisha as she explored her future on the druidic path. But she would not be doing all of that on her own.

“We’ve got some amazing guests, Celia Rose Gooding and Abubakar Salim," Iyengar told Polygon. "Two people who I have admired for so long; it was so fun to finally sit down and play with them. And, of course, the return of Travis Willingham and his new PC.”

Willingham has been absent from Critical Role’s Campaign 4 since his katari Paladin, Teor Pridesire, died in episode 30. Teor was killed inside House Tachonis’s Obrimus Manor during a truly heartbreaking moment for the fans and the cast.

Gooding and Salim have both guest-starred on Critical Role before: Gooding appeared in Exandria Unlimited: Divergence as the half-elf Rei’nia Saph, while Salim has played various roles, most recently the fungril Berserker Mercy in Age of Umbra: Sallowlands.

Though Iyengar couldn’t reveal what characters Willingham and the other guests would play in this two-episode arc, she told Polygon they were all “deeply connected and bound by a similar purpose.”

“Dol-Runja is the seat of the orcs and the druids in Kahan. So it's important and interesting to see multiple facets of that.”

Since June, the Seekers and Schemers tables have been dealing with assassination attempts at the theater, watery heists, and literal hell. When we last checked in, the Seekers table — with the help of several NPCs like fey pixie Clauny the Rose, talking dog Dame Morgaine, and scoundrel Pimley Morn — successfully rescued their ally turned into stone, Ulbid Morn.

On Dec. 3, Critters will reunite with Thaisha, who set off for the city of Dol-Rungja. There, she hopes to speak with the Druidic people and persuade them to abandon their neutrality and help fight back against the Sundered Houses.

Whether that will work out for Thaisha remains to be seen. The last time she encountered other druids, a few of them weren’t too pleased with her role in bringing the Necromancer Wizard, Occtis Tachonis (Alexander Ward), back to life as a Hollowed One. Given that she’ll have to answer for it to very important people, including her grandma, we expect the orc druid to be put through the proverbial wringer over the course of her two-episode arc.

#3341. 'Ghost Accounts' Are Putting Your Security at Risk, but You Can Protect Yourself

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

In all the years you've been online, you've likely created more accounts than you can remember, whether to shop on a website you made one purchase from, sign up for a newsletter you've since stopped reading, or download apps for school or work that you no longer need.

These so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways. That's why it's important to go through the effort to find and delete dormant accounts. Here's how to get started.

As McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords. While this doesn't mean your information is sure to be compromised, the more places it lives, the more opportunities there are for bad actors to get ahold of it.

You're less likely to be keeping tabs on activity in older accounts, which may also have weak or reused passwords that haven't been updated in years. If that company or service experiences a data breach, not only is your stored data there exposed, but that information (including your password) can be used to access other accounts using tactics like credential stuffing and phishing. This also increases the risk of identity theft, as threat actors can use your name, birth date, and other information to open fraudulent accounts.

Unfortunately, finding and removing forgotten accounts can be tedious. If you have a password manager, the easiest way to start is to audit older items as well as look at security reports that identify weak or reused passwords, as well as data breaches that have impacted your accounts. If you've saved credentials in your browser keychain, go through the same process to find dormant accounts.

The next place to look is in your email: Search for account confirmation and verification emails as well as password resets using keywords like "verify your email," "free trial," "welcome," "confirm your account," or "sign up." Add a date filter to narrow down older accounts. Do this across all of your email addresses.

Once you've found accounts you no longer use, the next step is to deactivate or delete them, which you may be able to do through the settings or by reaching out to customer support. At the very least, remove all identifying information and change the password, and if possible, update the address to a burner using your browser's or password manager's hide-my-email feature. If you no longer have access to an old account, that doesn't mean it's been deactivated and your information removed, so you may need to reach out to customer support to find out how to access and delete it.

#3340. Every Version of 'A Christmas Carol,' Ranked (and Where to Stream Them)

Charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol is the greatest story about Christmas ever written—even better than the one with Mary and Joseph and the manger. The 1843 tale of a miser browbeaten by self-righteous ghosts is (probably) the most filmed story of all time. Dozens of cinematic adaptations of A Christmas Carol have been released in theaters and on TV since Scrooge; or Marley's Ghost came out in 1901. Hundreds or thousands if you count re-imaginings and very special episodes of sitcoms. But which version is the very best?

I've carefully considered every major theatrical and TV adaptation of A Christmas Carol and rated each in terms of holiday spirit, Dickensian whimsy, and Scrooge-osity to arrive at the definite, no-argument-possible best-to-worst list of Christmas Carols.

To rank Christmas Carols, you have to decide what A Christmas Carol is to you. My criteria for inclusion: It has to be full-length (at least around an hour long); it has to have been released widely, either in theaters, on network television, or through a larger streaming service, and it has to be fairly close to a direct adaptation—modernizations, re-imaginings, sequels, and that episode of The Six Million Dollar Man don’t count (sorry, Scrooged fans). Using those criteria, I’ve winnowed the Carols down to the 17 you see below, ranked from best to worst, along with where you can stream each one.

It's tough to pick a single adaptation of A Christmas Carol as the absolute best of all time, but the 1984 TV movie version starring George C. Scott is unassailable. Other versions do some things better, but this one does everything right—no mistakes. It stays close to the original text; it's perfectly produced; and it has a consistency of tone and vision that makes it the most balanced of all versions of the story. A Christmas Carol might not have the best Scrooge of all time, but George C. Scott's performance is a solid nine out of ten, and this version features the most adorable and pitiable Tiny Tim of all and the best Ghost of Christmas Present, played by Edward Woodward, who played the policeman in The Wicker Man.

Shot in the midst of the Great Depression, the first sound version of A Christmas Carol digs deeper into the despair and horror of the story than any other adaptation. It’s a bleak, German expressionist Christmas flick, and Seymour Hicks’ sickly, haunted portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge fits the tone perfectly. Instead of delighting in his own crapulence, Hicks plays Scrooge like Satan in The Divine Comedy—he's not the ruler of Hell; he's its most tormented prisoner. Scrooge's miserliness is played as pathology. He wears dirty, torn clothing and shivers miserably while eating gruel because he can’t bring himself to burn a single scrap of coal. Even when he converts, it seems like a manic episode instead of Christmas spirit, suggesting this could be a story about an old man going mad.

Where to stream: Sadly, the version on free streaming services like Tubi and Plex is colorized, but you can watch it on YouTube in glorious black and white.

This big-budget musical take on the Yuletide classic turns Dickens up to 11. Scrooge is huge, a raucous, crowd-pleasing musical with hundreds of extras, elaborate sets, and a scenery-chewing central performance from Albert Finney to hold it all together. But Finney and company also manage to keep the emotional core of the story intact. The music is great, with memorable tunes like “I Hate People,” a song that Finney snarls instead of sings. Scrooge has the best ghosts of any version of A Christmas Carol, too—you can't beat the cheesy awesomeness of big-money 1970s special effects.

Before Hallmark devoted its corporate life to forgettable holiday-themed romantic comedies, it co-produced one of the best versions of A Christmas Carol ever made. This entire movie belongs to Patrick Stewart, whose nuanced, layered portrayal of Scrooge is the best that has ever been done. His "conversion" scene is so visceral and honest, it brought a tear to my eyes, even though I've seen the exact scene performed in at least 40 other movies, stage plays, and episodes of 1980s sitcoms. Sadly, the paucity of basic cable budgets in the 1990s results in some chintzy-looking sets and laughable special effects that mar an otherwise top-notch production.

Horror director Ti West's Carol adaptation muddies the moral clarity of Dickens' tale and suggests there's something deeply troubling beneath all the Victorian holiday catharsis. With a few exceptions, Ebenezer hits the familiar beats of A Christmas Carol: It delivers the crowd-pleasing rich-jerk-turns-good story moviegoers expect, but West layers in subtle hints along the way that suggest the floorboards are rotten, and if you dance with Christmas joy too hard, you'll fall into the dark basement below. Ebenezer seems to whisper to audiences, "How much does the conversion of one miserly wretch matter in the face of systemic injustice? And isn't he going to snap out of it when the fright wears off anyway?" Bonus: As you'd probably expect from a Ti West movie, the ghosts are genuinely scary.

I'm sticking A Muppet Christmas Carol randomly here on the list because you can't reasonably compare it to other versions of the story. The Muppet version is a thing unto itself. Like the Ol' Dirty Bastard, its style has no father. A Muppet Christmas Carol is absolutely delightful from start to finish, for children, grown-ups, cats, dogs, space aliens, and anything else you got. It shouldn't even work to set Michael Caine's serious portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge against a supporting cast of puppets, but somehow it all seems natural.

Alastair Sim takes Ebenezer Scrooge on a real journey in this movie. In the first act, he plays Scrooge like Capitalism personified, an uncaring, amoral monument to pure acquisition. He seems like a Scrooge who'd scare away ghosts, but when Marley shows up dragging his trademark chains, Sim is instantly reduced to pop-eyed fear, like the single chink in his armor is the supernatural. Scrooge then regresses to a childlike, bashful figure as ghosts lead him to different visions, finally emerging from his symbolic death to his rebirth as a Christmas-obsessed guy who lives to serve others. This movie might be among the best of the genre, but an unnecessary subplot about Scrooge's business sandbags the movie through part of the second act.

Mr. Magoo's Christmas Carol was the first animated version of A Christmas Carol and the first animated holiday special ever shown on American TV. The main character, Mr. Magoo, was the star of a one-joke, limited-animation cartoon popular in the early 1960s about an old man who couldn’t see very well, so it’s surprising how carefully crafted and effective this version of A Christmas Carol is. It's weirdly meta too: Jim Backus voices Mr. Magoo, who is a (blind) actor performing as Scrooge in A Christmas Carol on Broadway, so the play is bookended with "this guy can't see!" bits. The songs are strange, memorable and funny (listen to "Razzleberry Dressing" above once and you'll never forget it), but the emotional core of the story remains surprisingly powerful. Jim Backus is amazing.

I'm breaking my own rule about not including shortened versions of the story because this animated Carol is that great. Its evocative, graceful, hand-drawn look belongs to animation legend Richard Williams and was inspired by the illustrations from the original version of A Christmas Carol. It's a cartoon, but it's not a kiddie cartoon, so the darkness of the ghosts isn't glossed over. Plus, Scrooge is voiced by Alastair Sim, reprising his role from 1951's Scrooge.

There's nothing wrong with this brightly lit, by-the-numbers take on A Christmas Carol, but it seems designed to appeal to as broad an audience as possible, so the rough edges of the story have been sanded off. The ghosts aren’t that scary. Scrooge isn’t that miserly, etc. It’s fine for a Christmas movie to be lighthearted fun, but the lowered stakes ultimately blunt the emotional resonance of the climax, leading to a mediocre Christmas Carol.

I'm including this version of A Christmas Carol because it's Lifehacker editor Meghan Walbert's favorite. Sorry, Meghan, but this flimsy 1970s TV movie adaptation hasn't aged well. Henry Winkler does a good job as Scrooge, and it's cool to see Burgess Meredith and other old-timey stars, but overall, this is a schmaltzy, plodding film that unwisely replaces a lot of Dickens' best writing with the work of 1970s TV hacks.

Where to stream it: Pluto, Tubi, Amazon Prime

I really wanted to like Disney’s A Christmas Carol. Robert Zemeckis is a great director and Jim Carrey is a force of nature, but I couldn't get through it. There might be a lot to recommend this version of the story, but using 2009’s technology to create realistic-looking characters was such a puzzling choice. The whole movie looks like a video game cutscene from a PS3 game, and I kept wanting to hit “A” to skip ahead to the gameplay.

It doesn't seem like the producers of this obscure 2012 straight-to-streaming feature had much money to work with, which is too bad. If they had, they might have been able to better realize some of the intriguing ideas behind this movie. It's a straight-up horror take on the tale, but it just isn't scary. Sadly, you can't carry a feature film on good intentions. Overall, a swing and a miss.

The animation in this 1997 musical cartoon version of A Christmas Carol is dated, pedestrian, and ugly. The songs are forgettable, and Scrooge has a pet bulldog for some reason. (The one good joke is that he named his dog "Debit.") It’s just not good, which is a shame, because the cast is overflowing with talent, including Tim Curry as Scrooge, Ed Asner, and Whoopi Goldberg.

This BBC drama goes for a philosophical, moody version of Scrooge, but it doesn’t come together. It’s dark, grim, and so ponderously self-serious that it collapses under its own weight. In an effort to present aspects of A Christmas Carol that haven't been seen before (like "How Marley got his chains"), A Christmas Carol rewrites the original text from the ground up, but it comes across like Dickens' first draft with a bad case of Surf Dracula.

The current state of Dickens adaptation is not good. Netflix's uninspired, sappy, CGI version of A Christmas Carol tries to tart the story up with slapstick, songs, and jokes, but it’s all cynical, lowest-common-denominator horseshit. The dialogue has been dumbed down and joked up. Scrooge has a silly dog for comic relief. They added scatological humor. Think about this: The minds behind Scrooge: A Christmas Carol read Dickens and concluded, “This story would be better with a wacky dog and fart jokes.”

A Christmas Carol is such a solid story, even a grade-school production of it can be fun to watch. But a cynical production of it is extra terrible, given the message of the story. This terrible ego project is a bottom-of-the-barrel Christmas Carol because it feels like a money grab. Kelsey Grammer sucks as Scrooge, mugging his way through a lightweight performance. Jason Alexander sucks as Marley. Jennifer Love Hewitt is, well, actually pretty good as Scrooge’s Christmas-past romantic interest. She is a rare bright spot in this dreary movie, however. Everything else is mid to terrible. It’s shot and lit like a TV show; the sets are bland and the songs forgettable. Overall, it has the cynical feeling of assembly-line, “let’s get this shit over with” TV production.

#3339. UK court rules Apple can share the top secret order everyone already knew

The Investigatory Powers Tribunal – essentially a British court that deals with complaints about state surveillance – has ruled that Apple is allowed to reveal a secret order it received from the UK government.

Apple had already found a clever way to alert British customers to the classified order without breaking the law, but it can now confirm what we all already knew, and talk openly about the issue …

In 2025, the British government ordered Apple to create a backdoor to allow access by security services and law enforcement. Even worse, the order was issued under legislation that prohibits companies from revealing that they have received this demand.

This would have meant that British customers who enabled ADP would think that their data was safe when in fact it wasn’t. As we’ve said many times before, any backdoor created for use by the good guys is vulnerable to discovery and exploitation by the bad guys.

“Apple can no longer offer Advanced Data Protection (ADP) in the United Kingdom to new users and current UK users will eventually need to disable this security feature. ADP protects iCloud data with end-to-end encryption, which means the data can only be decrypted by the user who owns it, and only on their trusted devices. We are gravely disappointed that the protections provided by ADP will not be available to our customers in the UK […] As we have said many times before, we have never built a backdoor or master key to any of our products or services and we never will.”

Tell me you’ve been ordered to create a backdoor to ADP without telling me you’ve been ordered to create a backdoor to ADP …

The UK government must admit that it issued a secret order to Apple to allow it access to encrypted customer data, a court has ruled […] The Home Office has “not established that it would be damaging to national security” to reveal that Apple had received a “technical capability notice” (TCN), the tribunal said. The ruling means that […] “much” of Apple and the non-profits’ legal challenge can now take place in open court.

One of the great ironies is that most people had never heard of ADP until the government effectively made it headline news in the tech press three years after it launched – a classic example of the Streisand Effect.

This ruling is a win both for transparency and commonsense. To be clear, the actual requirement for a backdoor remains in place, but this can now be challenged in open court.

#3338. 17 Greek Mythology Books For Adult Percy Jackson Fans

Dani Kessel Odom (they/them) is an autistic lead writer and TV critic who covers sci-fi shows like Doctor Who and Pluribus, fantasy shows like The Magicians and Percy Jackson, and horror of all kinds. They also cover Marvel and DC TV shows and movies, with a robust knowledge of comic books. Their TV reviews can be found on Rotten Tomatoes.

Dani is also part of ScreenRant's books team, using their fiction writing and literature studies as the backbone for their book analyses.

They have covered events, such as the Denver Fan Expo. Professionals in the field, such as Damien Leone and Lucy Hale, have shared their articles. Their review of Ponies was quoted in the show's TV trailer.

In university, they majored in English Writing with a minor in psychology. They have always had a passion for analyzing TV and movies, even taking filmography and scriptwriting classes in university. They also studied and participated in onstage and onscreen acting extensively from the ages of 7 to 18.

Aside from working at Screen Rant, Dani has worked as a freelance editor and writer over the past decade, often in a ghostwriting capacity.

Percy Jackson & The Olympians is one of the most popular Greek mythology book series since the turn of the century, which is saying something because our fascination with the old stories has never completely ceased. The stories continue to be reimagined, whether on the screen or in books, every day. However, there’s something unique and special about the Percy Jackson books. Luckily, it’s a great time to be a fan.

Rick Riordan continues to expand the Riordanverse, which includes Percy Jackson and other mythological series like the Kane Chronicles, all the time. Plus, the story is back on the TV screen. Disney+’s Percy Jackson season 3 has received overwhelmingly positive reviews, with special praise for its fight sequences and its darker tone.

What’s more, publishers have noticed Percy Jackson's popularity over the past two decades, and they’ve catered to fans of this series and general Greek mythology lovers. Plenty of books exist that are perfect for Percy Jackson fans who read them when they were younger and are now adults. These seventeen stand out for their spirit of adventure, their imagination, and their ability to capture Greek myths in new ways.

One of the most thrilling parts of the Percy Jackson books is that they put Greek mythology and characters into our world, rather than taking the reader back to their world. These modern books function on the same principle, imagining how the Greek gods and their children would fare if they existed nowadays. Lightning & Thunder, which I’ve had the chance to read ahead of its release, has a more optimistic view of that prospect, while Gods Behaving Badly has a darkly comedic view of the gods struggling. Either way, though, it's extremely entertaining.

Stone Blind by Natalie Haynes, Andromeda by E.S. McLeod, Clytemnestra by Costanza Casati, Circe by Madeline Miller, I, Medusa by Ayana Gray

Many of the best retellings of Greek myths center on overlooked, villainized characters, matching Percy Jackson’s core values. The series has always been about outsiders, and Rick Riordan amplifies voices of characters typically silenced. What’s more, he encourages empathy for characters like Luke, who could easily be dismissed as villains. These five are standout choices.

The Games Gods Play by Abigail Owen, Blood of Hercules by Jasmine Mas, ODY-C by Matt Fraction & Christian Ward, Arch-Conspirator by Veronica Roth

Some of the most thrilling examples of Greek mythology books place the gods and heroes in an entirely new fantasy or science fiction setting. It’s a fun thought experiment. How would these characters we know and love fare in a different world. This leads to entertaining high-stakes stories like The Games Gods Play and Blood of Hercules, where the characters are underdogs trying to survive. Meanwhile, ODY-C and Arch-Conspirator not only reimagines the gods but also the technology of the world. Luckily, they all share the same spirit of adventure as Percy Jackson, but with adult maturity.

Now is the perfect time to dive into The Games Gods Play and the rest of Abigail Owen's The Crucible series because the third book in the series, The Wrath Gods Reap, came out just this month, and it is the best book of the series. It's faster-paced, higher-stakes, and it finally gives readers an emotional payoff that's 3 books in the making.

A Thousand Ships by Natalie Haynes, The Song of Achilles by Madeline Miller, The End Crowns All by Bea Fitzgerald, Troy: Lord of the Silver Bow by David Gemmell

The Iliad and The Odyssey are probably the most popular Greek myths in existence, continually being brought to the screen or the page in new ways. Even Percy Jackson had its own take on the latter epic poem with Sea of Monsters. These four books offer new perspectives and fun adventures that will be perfect for folks who want more adventure and tension.

#3337. The 6 Most Outrageous GTA 6 Myths, Debunked

The internet is already drowning in GTA 6 misinformation

After a wild opening weekend, Grand Theft Auto 6 is off to the races. Millions are playing Rockstar’s enormous open-world game and discovering its complexities in real time. There’s a lot to unpack in a game that’s filled with intersecting gameplay systems across a long story, and some players are already taking advantage of that. At the same time, the opening days of GTA 6’s launch have been filled with misinformation, much of it fueled by culture warriors and content creators looking to turn outrage into clicks on social media platforms that incentivize such behavior.

Because of that, there are a lot of myths about GTA 6 currently floating around the internet. Some come from harmless misunderstandings, while others are more deliberate misrepresentations intended to scare off potential players. To help you navigate the noise, we’ve rounded up some of the most rampant myths currently circulating around GTA 6 and fact-checked them accordingly.

The claim: GTA 6’s story forces you to do chores for Lucia instead of crimes.

If you spent launch day watching reactions to GTA 6’s early hours roll in instead of playing, you might have walked away thinking that Rockstar made a chore simulator. That’s thanks to a few early missions that revolve around Jason getting his home ready for Lucia as she’s about to be released from prison. Players will paint a bedroom for her, fix a leaky roof, and repair some stairs. There’s also an optional quest where players can run errands to prepare for Lucia's arrival, like picking up groceries or buying her a necklace. All of this happens in the first few hours of the game. GTA 6 quickly ramps up after that, getting into the series’ usual flow of cop chases, heists, and shootouts. You can call it a slow start, but know that any mundane missions you’ve seen make up a very small amount of story that you’re likely to see in your very first play session.

The claim: GTA 6 doesn’t allow you to steal cars, or heavily restricts what you can steal.

While there’s a grain of truth to this, it has been heavily exaggerated on social media. There are some select cars that you can’t steal in GTA 6, like those around Jason’s neighborhood or in an NPC’s car lot. But for the most part, you can jack just about any vehicle you see in Leonida. The catch is that you’ll need a device that can copy keys to get into some of the more expensive cars, and you won’t get that until Chapter 3. Being able to steal anything requires some patience as you play through the story, but be rest assured that you can do as much grand theft auto as ever in Grand Theft Auto.

The claim: Airplanes will bounce off of buildings instead of exploding on impact.

This one is a little tricky to unpack because there seem to be two weird things colliding here. After videos of airplanes bouncing off of skyscrapers like rubber began to emerge on social media, players deduced that content creators were sharing videos where they had their Reduced Vehicle Damage setting turned on. It seemed like a textbook case of outrage farming, though there may be a slight bit of truth here. Some players have speculated that GTA 6 may have a few physics bugs that make it tough for certain airliners to blow up as expected. That may be an edge case, but I can confirm that I have crashed plenty of planes into buildings in GTA 6, and they have all exploded into a fiery wreck so far.

The claim: GTA 6 features no autosave, and you will lose progress if you don’t manually save.

When players started reporting that they were losing hours of gameplay because GTA 6 didn’t have an autosave feature, I was very confused. I can open my save file right now and see a dedicated auto save slot that is regularly refreshed as I play. I initially wrote it off as players either lying or not realizing that the auto save only triggers after completing major missions, but it turns out they weren’t hallucinating. GTA 6’s first patch fixed an issue where auto save wasn’t triggering properly. So, yes, GTA 6 does have autosave; it just wasn’t working correctly for some players at launch. It shouldn’t be a problem now, but always remember to save early and often just in case.

The claim: Lucia is cheating on Jason during the story.

This one is downright bizarre. One of the first talking points that came out about GTA 6 was that Jason is a “cuck” who does not realize that Lucia is cheating on him. As someone who has played through the story, I spent days trying to figure out where in the world that blatant lie could be coming from. It turns out it was a good old misinterpretation. Early in the story, Lucia sends a text to an unknown character, which she rushes to hide from Jason when he enters the scene. While some have interpreted that as Lucia having a secret lover, it actually turns out that she was texting a friend from prison. To players’ credit, the scene does feel like it’s built to make you think Lucia is hiding a big secret from Jason, so that reaction might have been exactly what Rockstar was hoping to provoke.

The claim: GTA 6 does not allow you to open fire and kill people in a gay club.

The ugliest rumor to come out of GTA 6 so far is that the game will not allow you to walk into a gay club in Vice City and kill people. There was even a clip going around social media that seemed to support that, sparking some grotesque reactions. The truth is that the location in the video isn’t specifically a gay club. It is a club, and it’s true that you can’t open fire in it, but that’s only because you can’t shoot inside any establishment in GTA 6. This claim would technically be true if there was a gay club in the game, but only as a side effect of the wider systems working the way they do. What is true, though, is that the game features an unkillable non-binary character, according to the actor who portrayed them.

This isn't a moral or ethical issue — boringly, it's about regulation

#3336. Shawn Levy and 21 Laps Set Overall Film Deal at Sony Pictures

Sony Pictures has won the services to one of the most in-demand commercial directors working today, Shawn Levy. Levy and his 21 Laps banner have signed a major first look overall film deal with Sony Pictures, with Sony beating out multiple studios in what’s said to be a competitive process.

Levy will develop and produce theatrical films through the 21 Laps Entertainment banner as part of the deal, which begins fall 2027 and extends across all Sony Pictures labels, so presumably that could include labels like Screen Gems or even Sony Animation. It’s a producing deal, not for directing, but we wouldn’t be surprised if that ends up being the case with one that his team brings in. Related Stories Steven Spielberg Directing His First Western with Paul Thomas Anderson Writing the Script ‘Focker In-Law’ Review: An Eager Ariana Grande Isn’t Enough to Save a Comedy Sequel That Can’t Remember What People Liked About This Franchise

This film deal comes after Levy and 21 Laps as recently as September signed a new overall TV deal with Disney’s 20th Television, with him exiting his Netflix deal. That pact doesn’t begin until October 2027.

Levy is reuniting with Sony’s leadership Tom Rothman and Sanford Panitch after he previously directed the “Night at the Museum” movies, “Cheaper by the Dozen,” and “Date Night” for them while they were all at Fox.

“I go ALL the way back with Shawn. We made a pile of hits together before he went on to far greater successes, none of which surprised me in the slightest,” Sony Pictures Motion Picture Group Chairman and CEO Tom Rothman said in a statement. “His talent as a producer, director and head of the coolest creative company around, is rivaled only by his unmatched enthusiasm. I feel lucky as hell to reunite, and excited for everyone at Sony to discover what I have long known — Shawn Levy is the real deal.”

“Tom, Sanford and I have a long history together, and some of the most formative and rewarding experiences of my career came during the years we worked together at Fox,” Levy said in a statement. “Tom saw the future of my career before I did, and he bet on me early and with a bighearted (and loud!) conviction that is one of his trademarks, and for which I’ll be forever grateful. 21 Laps was built on empowering fellow filmmakers and helping them tell stories imbued with their unique voices and visions. Along with my entire 21 Laps team, I’m thrilled to begin this next chapter with the team at Sony, and am excited about the wide-open breadth of opportunity across Sony’s many labels. I deeply value their commitment to theatrical filmmaking.”

While just about everyone else in Hollywood has taken a victory lap with the success of “Backrooms,” you may have forgotten that Levy and 21 Laps were producers on the A24 horror movie, and he of course directed and produced Netflix’s “Stranger Things,” which concluded at the end of last year. Up next for Levy is “Star Wars: Starfighter,” which is a “Star Wars” spinoff starring Ryan Gosling and which opens May 28, 2027. And he’s also teaming with Gosling and Disney yet again on Marvel’s “Ghost Rider,” which opens July 28, 2028. His last feature he directed was “Deadpool & Wolverine,” which made $1.3 billion worldwide.

On the 21 Laps side, the banner is producing a rom-com with Emma Stone and Chris Pine set at Universal called “The Catch;” Netflix’s drama series “The Sticks,” starring Michelle Monaghan; Amazon MGM Studios’ supernatural horror film “Seasons;” Netflix’s feature comedy “One Attempt Remaining,” starring Jennifer Garner and John Cena; and an untitled Netflix spy feature starring Kevin Hart and Henry Cavill.

Shawn Levy and 21 Laps Entertainment are represented by WME and Wendy Kirk at JSSK.

#3335. iOS 27.3 beta can cause HomeView issues, Apple confirms

Apple’s new HomeView just launched last Friday, but some early adopters reported issues with Siri AI in their first days of use. Apple shipped fixes in HomeView 27.2.1 yesterday, but it also confirmed the iOS 27.3 beta is responsible for some of the problems.

Yesterday Apple released its first post-launch software update for HomeView, less than a week after the product debuted.

Per the company’s official release notes, HomeView 27.2.1 focuses on bug fixes, including a fix for the following issue:

Pairing with an iPhone or iPad running the iOS or iPadOS 27.3 beta may cause Siri requests to fail

It’s unknown how many reports of Siri issues on HomeView can be attributed to the iOS 27.3 beta. However, it wouldn’t surprise me if many of the reports were from beta users. That’s in part because early HomeView reviewers didn’t seem to have the same problems.

With HomeView 27.2.1 now available, those problems should hopefully be taken care of. However, if you’re on the iOS 27.3 beta, there’s a new issue you’ll need to deal with temporarily.

As discovered by pdfu, if you try to make a Personal Content request on an iPhone running iOS 27.3, Siri in HomeView 27.2.1 now says: “I can’t help with that because your personal device is on newer software.”

If you’re on iOS 27.3, Siri on HomeView can’t use your iPhone for personal context, likely until December.HomeView won’t send Siri requests to an iPhone on newer software. Without a HomeView update, your only option is iOS 27.2.x.On-device requests like timers still work. https://t.co/8UbRs7z496

It’s understandable that issues might arise from having iOS and HomeView software that’s out of sync. Unfortunately though, there’s no beta software available for HomeView at the moment.

That means unless Apple releases a beta soon, users might have to wait until the public launch of HomeView 27.3 in December to get Personal Content features back.

#3334. The Best Tech Deals From the Sam's Club Early Black Friday Sale

Retailers are churning out early Black Friday deals already, including the likes of Amazon, Best Buy, Walmart, and others. If you're waiting around for Friday, Nov. 27 to do all of your shopping, you might miss out on some deals and unnecessarily make the day more stressful than it needs to be. If you're a Sam's Club member, you have access to many early Black Friday deals worth checking out. I spent some time combing through their website and rounded up my favorite tech deals below.

The Bose SoundLink Flex SE is a portable Bluetooth speaker with an IP67 waterproof rating. The speaker even floats in the water, so you can bring it with you into the pool. While it doesn't offer full EQ customization in its companion app, the sound has rich bass depth and clear highs out of the box. It also features a speakerphone, allowing you to take calls and speak with it. It's light and portable, and the Bluetooth 5.3 supports multipoint connectivity and SBC, AAC, and aptX codecs. You can get the Bose 2nd Generation SoundLink Flex SE for $89 (originally $139).

Skullcandy makes fun speakers and headphones, although they're not designed for audiophiles (their sound signature is very bass-heavy). Their Skullcandy Stomp XL Max is their attempt at making a portable party speaker. It comes with two wireless mics, making it a great option for karaoke. It holds 12 hours of battery life (up to 20 hours with certain settings), has an IPX5 water resistance rating, and has LED lights that sync to the music. You can get it for $99 (originally $199).

Getting a soundbar can exponentially improve anyone's entertainment system, but a 5.1 system with rear speakers and a subwoofer takes it to the next level. The Samsung HW-Q65F 5.1 Channel Soundbar is $299 (originally $399), and it's a wireless setup that will keep the harmony of "too many cables" in the house. It supports Dolby Atmos and DTS Virtual:X to give you a 3D audio feel, and it has a dialogue feature that will let you hear the whispers.

Gaming monitors can get expensive quickly, but you can get decent options on a budget. A great example is the 31.5-inch MSi gaming monitor selling for $129 (originally $179). It has a 250Hz refresh rate and a 1ms response time to make gaming smoother. There's also AMD FreeSync Premium to get rid of tearing and stuttering.

These kinds of sales are always a good time to upgrade laptops. If you're looking for a powerful computer that is well-rounded, consider the 16-inch HP OmniBook 7 Flip going for $699 (originally $899). This laptop comes with an Intel Ultra 5 processor, 512GB of SSD, and 16GB of RAM (which, honestly, is the minimum anyone should be buying in 2026).

If you need a bigger screen, the 17.3-inch HP OmniBook 3 is a good choice for a bit less money. It comes with an Intel Core Ultra 7 processor, 512GB of SSD, and 12GB of RAM. Part of the bigger screen means a bigger keyboard, so if you deal with numbers a lot, you'd likely appreciate the numeric pad.

If you want your laptop strictly for gaming, the ASUS TUF F16 Gaming laptop is $1,149 (originally $1,399). With an Intel Core 7 processor and the RTX 5060 graphics card, you'll be well set up to tackle heavy games. It comes with a 165Hz refresh rate, Advanced Arc Flow fans and vents to keep your machine cool, and 16GB DDR5 RAM to keep your loads short.

Budget TVs get big discounts during Black Friday, and the 58-inch Vizio QLED TV is one of them. You can get one for $178 (originally $298), and it supports Dolby Vision HDR for better color and contrast. The operating system is the Vizio OS, but of course, you can always change it with a TV dongle if you prefer a different one.

If you prefer to splurge for a better QLED but still get a good deal, the 65-inch Samsung QN90H QLED TV at $1,197.99 (originally $1,497.99) is a great option. It upscales lower-resolution pictures to 4K with AI. It works for gaming with its 144Hz refresh rate, and because the operating system is Tizen OS, it comes with Samsung TV Plus, which brings over 2,700 free channels. The TV also comes with Dolby Atmos, so you can hear audio with a 3D effect as the audio follows objects around the display.

A 100-inch TV makes a statement: You take your entertainment system seriously. The 100-inch Vizio QLED TV is a budget-friendly option with a $300 discount, currently going for $1,198 (originally $1,498). This TV supports Dolby Vision HDR for more vivid images and has hundreds of free channels with the Vizio OS.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

#3333. ‘Cliff Booth’ Star Elizabeth Debicki on Slapping Brad Pitt, ‘The Movie Critic,’ and the Rom-Com Question

Don’t let the title fool you: “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” might offer up a breezy, very fun-to-watch new entry into the life and times of titular (and fictitious) Hollywood stuntman, but co-star Elizabeth Debicki steals the show in David Fincher’s film (in addition to stealing the heart of Brad Pitt’s Cliff). Is it time to greenlight “The New Adventures of Karen Crosby”? We think so.

The much-anticipated sequel to Quentin Tarantino’s “Once Upon in Hollywood” picks up nearly a decade after the Oscar-winning antics of the previous film, finding Cliff pursuing new professional endeavors (film projecting! bartending! contract killing, kind of!). Stunt work? Eh, only when he feels like, and he certainly feels like after taking an unexpected meeting with Hollywood agent Karen Crosby (Debicki), whose grace and good humor instantly delight both Cliff and the audience. Related Stories Shawn Levy and 21 Laps Set Overall Film Deal at Sony Pictures Steven Spielberg Directing His First Western with Paul Thomas Anderson Writing the Script

Tossed together by the wacky demands of Karen’s marquee client, actor Charlie Nelson (Scott Caan), the shaggy, Tarantino-penned “Cliff Booth” meanders its way through every corner of Hollywood, finding real emotional ballast and crackling chemistry every time Pitt and Debicki share the screen. Characteristically wordy and dense, we learn plenty about Karen along the way (including her early forays into film criticism and her current feelings about movies), and she wins Cliff’s heart by, well, literally and physically slapping the crap out of him.

Ahead, IndieWire catches up with the Aussie star (who gets to use her real accent this time) about Fincher’s film, from slapping her co-star to some serious ruminations on the instantly iconic “pig monologue speech.” No wonder Cliff went so crazy for Karen; she’s a delight.

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

IndieWire: What was your relationship with “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” when the film came out in 2019?

Elizabeth Debicki: I went to see it in the cinema. I think I went by myself, which makes me think I must have been on a job. I was definitely in the States, maybe I was in L.A., and I went one afternoon. I went and sat in the cinema, and I loved it. It’s really vivid in my memory.

I didn’t watch it again before we made this for performance reasons. In a way, I realized I didn’t really need to because, [there’s] something about Quentin’s movies, they just kind of wedge themselves in your brain. I can literally see the Playboy Mansion scene. I can see the Manson kids driving up to the house. I can see Margaret Qualley’s feet on the dashboard. I can see everything.

So it sounds like you came into this as a Tarantino fan.

And to get Tarantino and Fincher is this incredible two-for-one.

It’s funny, because obviously in the making of this, I had to sort of normalize that. And they helped me do that because they were, from the second I got onto set — which was a two-week rehearsal period where we really worked through the script — we had Quentin for that whole period. [It was] very, very collaborative.

A part of me wonders whether it was that thing where they have sat with the material for so long and had their full body relationship to it, and then I was fresh. I had my own thoughts and feelings. My memories of those rehearsal periods were really all three of them [Fincher, Tarantino, and Pitt] just turning to me and saying, “What do you think? What do you think?” The first time it happened, I was like, “Oh my God, what do I think?” After a little while, I started to actually say what I thought, which was great.

I didn’t audition for this. David emailed me and asked me if I would be interested in playing a part. I remember he phrased it in an email as he hoped that I would consider playing a very tricky part in a film he was hoping to make in July. It was a very David-ism kind of email. I think it said something like, “I hope you understand the seriousness of this conundrum,” or something. And I called him up and yeah, I was obviously ready to say, “I’ll do it.”

He was very, very insistent. He was like, “Wait, wait, wait. I really want to tell you everything about it.” Because at that point he and Quentin were doing a massive edit of the script. He couldn’t send it to me there and then.

Karen is so singular, but she is in a familiar position if you’re working in Hollywood. Did you base any part of your performance on any agents or managers or publicists that you know or have encountered?

When I first read the script, there were things that just rang so true to me, and might seem outrageous for anyone or slightly absurd maybe for anyone who doesn’t work in this industry. The incredible pig scene where Cliff talks about killing a pig, and then the scene in the car where Karen says, “Now because of you, I now have to spend my entire morning finding a pig. That is not a joke, that is literally what I have to get up and do. And you know what? I had a lot of things I had to do, and it wasn’t find a pig. And now I have to drive your ass all the way to Marina del Rey because I have to just deliver you because that’s what my client needed.”

It’s kind of this absurd ask, but it’s folded into “that’s what I need for my process.” Quentin and David, they’re so fascinating because they are Hollywood. They are Hollywood, and also they sit outside it, and they observe it from these very, very unique vantage points. Quentin, in particular, his love affair with L.A. is so profound, and with Hollywood. Part of the thing I loved about her too is that she’s sort of accidentally an agent, which is not frequently do you come across that. One of the things too that feels very human about her is that she sort of had this other dream, but she took one really bad knock, and it broke her heart, and she just buried it deep inside and then made decisions based off that.

When we get to that scene with Karen and Cliff when you’re talking about how Karen had this other career as a film critic, I how much of that was lifted from what would’ve been Quentin’s movie, “The Movie Critic”?

I don’t know. I don’t actually know the answer to that question in terms of the parallel there. But I do love that in the middle of this film about 1977 in Hollywood, that there’s a really important moment where we think about Pauline Kael, and we think about her and she lives in this film. I’m so glad that there’s this moment where my character gets to say, “Pauline Kael is my god,” because she was. She was incredible.

As Karen, you have this great monologue explaining to Cliff who you used to be, what had happened with that career path, how wonderful it was that Pauline supported you, and then it didn’t work out. And then you have another monologue about seeing movies as hamburgers. It’s a really funny tension for Karen, because the audience likely assumes she loves movies and does see them as art.

That’s right, there is a tension there. I feel like one of the things that Quentin can do so well, and kind of totally unique to his own brain, is that he sort of plucks an idea out of the zeitgeist, something that we’re all thinking about, and he feeds it through his characters in a way that feels very organic. This is a big conversation that people are having as the industry shifts and changes. It also was a huge conversation that was happening in 1977. There was this big question of, “Is that art still if it’s commercial, if its box office success equates to this?” I think that the dichotomy of what she believes in her heart and wants to be true and what she spouts in front of people, I sort of think both things are true at once, and I think that’s just the kind of human element.

But I also think that it’s important to remember in that monologue that Charlie really pulls it out of her. She really doesn’t want to do the dance, the dancing monkey, or what did she say? “There’s a dancing bear aspect to your request,” I think is such a great line. But yeah, I think both things are true for her.

You have the sense she’s said this speech before, and again, maybe she doesn’t totally believe it, but Charlie just loves it and so she has to do it.

David and I spoke about it a lot, and we sort of landed on we feel like she did it once off the cuff, like at a table at the Emmys or the Globes, and everyone went, “Gee, Karen, that’s genius.” And Charlie heard it and went, “Yeah, that’s genius. She’s my agent, look how smart she is. She’s so great.” Then she’s done it one other time at a dinner. So, by the time we get to the pool, she’s like, “Oh, my God.” It’s becoming a routine against her will, which was also a really fun element to play with in terms of how much she does or doesn’t enjoy it, and finding that balance.

Do you personally read reviews of your work?

Has it always been the case? [Smiles] I’m sure anyone who doesn’t read a review once read a bad review.

It doesn’t even have to be a bad one. What I learned is, you can read a review that is seemingly positive, but it might not be what you were trying to do, and then you feel heartbroken about that too. So yes, I really avoid it. Yeah.

You get to slap Brad Pitt a lot in this film. Was that hard to do?

It’s a very beautiful face, and we had to do it. We had to do it. And Brad is a very good sport and a very good stuntman. I think that Brad was very, very comfortable, and I was very nervous. We shot the dialogue for two days, that we were just in almost this sort of trance of the two of them, and of the very unusual power dynamic that [they have]. One of the best things about that scene to me, which I didn’t analyze at the time, it’s so intricate the way that Quentin wrote it. It’s this moment where, in revealing what he wants, he becomes so vulnerable that the power dynamic kind of very subtly shifts in this kind of core foundational way between these two characters.

So, we shot that for two days and then all of a sudden it was like, “Oh, my God, it ends, and I need to figure out how to do this.” We had an amazing stunt coordinator on that job.

We had to do extremely complex things with people, but with me, I was like, “Hey Dave, could we just pop out the back there and have a little chat about the slap…?”

Everyone knows that David likes to do a lot of takes. How many takes was the actual slapping?

Not so many! It was probably the least amount of takes we did. We probably did a couple, five, maybe six. And then I do remember that Brad sort of went, “OK, I think we got it. I think we’re good now,” and we moved on. But we did the inside [slap] first. It was such a joy to do. It’s such a happy memory. We filmed it, and then we all ran around to the monitor, and we watched it in playback, and we’re like, “Oh, my God, it’s so good.” And then we filmed it again. We were so pleased with ourselves. [Laughs]

What scenes did David ask for the most takes?

The thing about the takes is, it’s coverage-dependent. So, if you have four actors in a scene, like the hamburger monologue, let’s say there’s four setups on each actor, you do 10 takes per setup. So, that becomes a lot.

I will say that in the pig speech monologue, I don’t have a lot of lines, but we did just as much coverage on me as we did on Brad and Scott. That was one of my first days on set, and I remember thinking, “This is so, so unusual. Why is he doing this?” And then a couple weeks later, he showed me a kind of rough edit, and I thought, “Oh, my God, that’s why he did it.” He is using Karen as the kind of go-between. As David would always say, at least there’s one grown-up in the room, and it’s Karen.

So I do have this really funny memory too of doing that during the pig monologue scene. I was off-camera, or we were catching just the side of me; I was very much out of focus, and I took a drag of the cigarette, and I remember he gave me a note for that, something about the speed of it or the intention of it. And I remember thinking …

Exactly! I was like, “You saw that?” And he was right, he was absolutely right, but I thought, “OK, this is not a set where we get away with anything.”

Especially in that scene, you have these facial expressions where you are having the appropriate reaction to what we’re hearing, but in such a beautiful way. I think that’s when we all fall in love with Karen. We’re like, “She gets it. She knows how ridiculous this is,” but she is part of this world.

I’m particularly proud of the Tic Tac crunch; that was my prop idea, and I just thought we should end with her crunching down on something, because she’s so pissed about having to then go and spend her entire morning looking for a hog in Malibu Colony or something. Where is she even going to find that pig?

She did it. I mean, David and I would talk about that too. I’m like, “Do you think she did it or she sent Mallory, her assistant, to go do it?” Either way, someone did it, someone paid for it.

Speaking of falling in love with Karen, there’s been this sentiment circulating as people see the film that there is a real rom-com built into it with Cliff and Karen. Do you see it that way?

I don’t think it’s a rom-com, but I think it’s romantic, and I think they’re funny. Don’t get me wrong, rom-coms are my religion. Yesterday I was walking through New York, and I literally felt like I was in “You’ve Got Mail.” I was like, “This fall day, I need a bunch of sharpened pencils.” But I don’t think that this necessarily falls into that category. It’s sort of undefinable, indefinable, but I do think it’s really romantic. I felt that when we were playing it, and we really enjoyed that together.

The romance of it is kind of surprising, because it surprises her. It’s sort of best case scenario romance, that you think you have it all together, and this person walks in that you absolutely dismiss in terms of that, and then little by little they just sort of reveal this thing. More beautifully, they pull something out of you. I didn’t necessarily intellectualize any of this while we were shooting it, it’s just that I can see that now retrospectively. Not that I read anything, but I am curious what people will make of them.

Netflix will release “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” in IMAX theaters on Wednesday, November 25. It will be available to stream on Netflix starting Wednesday, December 23.

#3332. Everything We Know About Spider-Man & Wolverine Being In Avengers: Doomsday

It's almost time for Avengers: Doomsday, and rumors swirl that Spider-Man and Wolverine will turn up. Marvel is determined to one-up even Avengers: Endgame, with this movie bringing back heroes from the last 26 years of Marvel blockbusters. The final Doomsday trailer divides its time between Steve Rogers and the X-Men, and even marked a franchise first: we finally got James Marsden's Cyclops saying an iconic line, "To me, my X-Men."

The X-Men, the Fantastic Four, and several different teams of Avengers are all going up against Robert Downey, Jr.'s Doctor Doom. But with the entire multiverse expected to end ahead of next year's Avengers: Secret Wars, we're all pretty certain there are going to be a lot more surprises. There have been particularly exciting rumors about both Spider-Man and Wolverine, but how likely are they to be true?

There's currently no evidence Tom Holland's Spider-Man is in Avengers: Doomsday. The core issue lies in the real-world, with the fact there are only small gaps in Holland's schedule where he could have been available for filming; he was occupied on The Odyssey through most of Doomsday's production, before moving on to Spider-Man: Brand New Day. If he does make an appearance at all, it would have to be a very small one indeed.

That said, there's intense debate about whether the end of Spider-Man: Brand New Day is actually Doomsday setup. It shows Ned Leeds' "Spider-Tracker" app losing Spider-Man completely, only to spot him in space. This is most likely a multiversal collision known as an incursion, where two different Earths collide. It's possible Holland's Spider-Man has been transported to another Earth, one that's about to impact Earth-616.

Tobey Maguire and Andrew Garfield both reprised their roles in Spider-Man: No Way Home, meaning they've already been part of the Multiverse Saga. It wouldn't be at all surprising to see them turn up; in fact, there have been rumors Doomsday kicks off with Maguire's Spider-Man killed in battle with the X-Men, who are fighting to save their universe. We'll have to wait and see whether that actually happens.

One thing's for sure: If Maguire or Garfield do return as Spider-Man in Avengers: Doomsday, it's likely to only be for a small role. The film principally involves three different Earths: Earth-616, the Fantastic Four's world, and the X-Men's. That already means Doomsday has a lot of cast to juggle (even more, given Doctor Doom may have been collecting people from other timelines as well). Many characters are likely to be relegated to cameos, just to make the story navigable.

Marvel is keeping very quiet about whether Hugh Jackman's Wolverine is in Doomsday. That said, the House of Ideas do seem intent on keeping Jackman on board till he's 90 (at least), and Deadpool and Wolverine brought the character into the Multiverse Saga. In this case, it feels likely Wolverine is being kept back as a surprise. But nobody will be shocked should Logan pop his claws and fight alongside the rest of the X-Men. Perhaps he's even one of the heroes who responds to Cyclops' call to arms in the trailer.

Speaking as a lifelong X-Men fan, I'm delighted to see other members of the team get the spotlight in Doomsday's marketing. Fox depended far too much on Wolverine's popularity, and it's been so good to see Marvel course-correct a little, choosing to emphasize the likes of Professor X and Cyclops. I'm sure there are going to be more X-Men surprises, too.

Oddly enough, though, there are actually quite a few heroes couldn't missing from Avengers: Doomsday's roll call. Sticking with the X-Men, two characters stand out: Ryan Reynold's Deadpool and Famke Janssen's Jean Grey. The former has already appeared in the Multiverse Saga, and even has connections to the Time Variance Authority. The latter is an absolute powerhouse (literally the Phoenix), so there's likely a story reason here. Perhaps Jean has already been killed (or recruited) by Doctor Doom.

Far too many heroes from Earth-616 are still absent. Brie Larson's Captain Marvel is surprising, again because she's one of the most powerful heroes in play. A multiversal event really should feature the "boss of space," so we can only hope she's going to turn up. Teyonah Parris' Spectrum was stranded in the X-Men timeline at the end of The Marvels, which should surely mean she's unwittingly triggering an incursion between Earth-616 and the X-Men universe. It would actually be rather odd for Marvel to ignore her in Doomsday.

The problem, of course, is that the MCU expanded a little too quickly during the Multiverse Saga. We were introduced to so many different superheroes; some are street level (such as Alaqua Cox's Echo), while others didn't prove especially popular (the less said about Secret Invasion's new Super-Skrulls, the better). Avengers: Doomsday already faces a huge challenge if it's to give due time to multiple Avengers teams as well as the X-Men, so some Earth-616 heroes are going to be neglected. Don't expect to see the Eternals anytime soon.

That said, Marvel did recently confirm two new heroes for Doomsday. Hailee Steinfeld is returning as Kate Bishop, meaning at least one of Marvel's two Hawkeyes (and, in this case, a Young Avenger in the comics) is due to appear. Meanwhile, VisionQuest's post-credits scene confirmed Doctor Doom has resurrected Elizabeth Olsen's Scarlet Witch, presumably confirming rumors Wanda Maximoff is one of the Latverian Witches we see in the recent trailer. If these two heroes are also back, then it's possible Marvel has quite a few surprises in the works. We'll find out more when Avengers: Doomsday finally releases in December.

The game takes place on Sunday, February 14, 2027, or Valentine’s Day 2027, and now you can convince your partner that the Valentine’s Day date night is still alive because you can go out to the movie theater to watch the game instead of stay at home.

IMAX will screen everything from the pregame and postgame coverage, the full four-hour presentation of the game itself, and of course the Halftime Show headlined by Jay-Z, all beginning at 6 pm ET. ESPN’s Monday Night Football broadcast team of Joe Buck, Troy Aikman, Lisa Salters, and Laura Rutledge will be the ones you hear in the theater, so no luck if you’re a Peyton and Eli or Pat McAfee fan. This is really a boon for theaters to do added business on a day and weekend when most theaters are pretty empty and the new movie options are few and far between. We’ll see though how the box office responds and how many people relocate their Super Bowl parties to their local multiplex.

“Watching the Super Bowl with your fellow fans is one of the great shared experiences in sports, and this first-of-its-kind collaboration with the NFL and IMAX takes it to a historic new scale,” said Ken Potrock, President, Major Event Integration for The Walt Disney Company. “With ESPN’s first Super Bowl, we’re reaching fans across an unprecedented range of platforms and meeting them wherever they want to be, with unique moments that only Disney and ESPN can deliver.”

“The Super Bowl is a one-of-a-kind global cultural event imbued with spectacle, sound, drama, and heroes — all the makings of a great IMAX experience,” said Rich Gelfond, CEO of IMAX. “This is a milestone for IMAX that further elevates our standing as a premier global platform for entertainment and events, and we’re excited to work in partnership with Disney, ESPN and the NFL to give football fans an unforgettable night.”

#3329. Microsoft To Do is retiring, including Mac and iOS apps

Microsoft is saying goodbye to its task management service To Do, including the Mac and iOS apps. Here’s what users need to know.

The last day to use the To Do apps is June 30, 2027. That date also applies to Windows, Android, and the web. The underlying service and sync support will retire later, according to Microsoft’s support document.

“Microsoft To Do is retiring,” Microsoft explains. “For work or school accounts, Microsoft Planner will be the destination for managing personal work tasks alongside assigned work. The updated My tasks experience begins rolling out in December 2026.”

On the Mac, you can use Planner on the web or in Teams. Microsoft explicitly says it has no plans for a native Mac app.

You can still see your existing To Do tasks in Planner through June 30, but your tasks and lists won’t carry over. Microsoft plans to offer an export option before the apps retire.

Planner doesn’t support personal Microsoft accounts however. If that’s how you use To Do, you’ll need to pick another task manager, even if you pay for Microsoft 365 Personal or Family, according to the company.

The June shutdown will end a run of just over a decade for To Do on Apple platforms. Microsoft bought the company behind Wunderlist in 2015 and released the first iPhone preview of To Do in April 2017.

Looking for a proper replacement? Apple’s built-in Reminders app can keep lists in sync between Apple devices, including a grocery list you share with family through iCloud.

Microsoft has been trying to make Teams as the super app for some time now, as Planner is integrated into Teams. Teams is one of the prime examples of why super apps are terrible, with a bloated, web app-like experience.

If you liked To Do because it worked across platforms, Todoist has apps for iPhone, iPad, Mac, Windows, and Android.

Does this sunsetting affect you? Were you a Wunderlist user back in the day? Share your thoughts in the comments.

Update: Howard Crow, Director of Product, Agents and AI, Microsoft, shared this statement with 9to5Mac regarding the transition:

“We’re bringing task management experiences together across Microsoft 365 to make it easier for customers to manage individual tasks and team plans. As part of this transition, Microsoft To Do apps will retire on June 30, 2027, with work and school experiences coming together in Microsoft Planner. Existing integrations across Microsoft 365, including Outlook and Teams, will also be updated to work with Planner. We recognize this change will affect customers differently, particularly those using personal Microsoft accounts, and we’re committed to helping them prepare. Customers will be able to export their To Do data before retirement, and we’ll share additional guidance to support the transition.”
