#3327. Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

You know “the look” by now. Every poster for a business or event has pictures of uncanny-looking people, buildings that don’t look right, and always that one font. But why? If generative AI is supposedly able to “think” and be “creative,” why do so many of its results come out looking exactly the same? The answer is complicated, and it has to do with what chatbots define as “thinking.”

At this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt. Some very fast models do, but most employ what’s known as “thinking models”, which are a bit of a misnomer. The “thinking” really just consists of generating a set of sub-prompts before executing the main one. And it’s in that hidden, generated text that most of the “choices” (to the extent that we can call the statistical output of an AI model a “choice”) occur that determine how a design looks.

To borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could). Most of this happens invisibly in the background, and many proprietary chatbots won’t show you their in-process “thinking” prompts even if you ask.

In the case of an AI poster, it might break down “make a poster” into smaller steps such as “create a design brief for a poster.” To demonstrate this while doing some testing for this piece, I added additional prompts for ChatGPT to explain the “design briefs” it generated, which included details like layout, colors, and typography.

The problem is those instructions are still subject to the same flaws as any other AI-generated text. They can’t properly fact-check; they can’t walk into the real world and see the thing they’re describing; and they can hallucinate or fall back on stale formats that become easy to notice after a while.

For example, while testing, I had ChatGPT generate a poster for a Lifehacker-themed nightclub. In every case, the underlying brief it generated outlined some basic details, but occasionally it added things I hadn’t asked for. This included additional text, iconography, and in one case it even added the “design brief” explanation I had requested as the bottom half of the poster.

Those mistakes filter into the final product, when the brief is then fed into the image generator that ultimately makes the poster. In my case, ChatGPT showed me the underlying explanations for its reasoning (though even that could be different from what was actually sent to the image generator), but most people who use a chatbot for this task won’t see these factors before getting the final result.

While most chatbots won’t show you exactly what underlying “thinking” they use, most can be coaxed into describing the vague outlines of how they reached certain outcomes. And those descriptions provide some insight into why certain chatbots keep outputting similar results over and over. It doesn’t take long for some patterns to emerge. For example, any prompt to generate a poster for a nightclub almost invariably generated a brief that had specifications for a color palette including “electric purple,” “electric yellow,” and “electric pink.”

The reason for this should be pretty obvious: When the statistical model underlying LLMs needs to come up with an example for “colors for a nightclub poster,” the most obvious answers are neon, high-energy colors. Unless you know something about the specific club’s vibe (and write that out and feed it to the chatbot), the AI will have to fill in the gaps with something. And that something will be based on the same statistics it uses to predict any word.

This pattern of repetition was everywhere in all the design rationale ChatGPT gave me. Across multiple attempts to generate a Club Lifehacker poster, the generated design brief added an overarching “concept” that described the fictional club’s atmosphere as “high-energy” and “futuristic.” Every bot mentioned using images with the “silhouette” of either the DJ or a dancing crowd (often both). All the text had to be “bold” and “futuristic."

If there's one dead giveaway that a poster was made with AI, it's that one brush-stroke font that they all seem to use. Now, this is a bit more speculative, but I have a theory on where that specific design comes from. And it’s worth noting upfront that this seems to only apply to posters generated by ChatGPT specifically.

One of the most common factors I found in my design brief testing was the use of phrases like “brush lettering” or “brush script.” Brush lettering is a design term that refers to using any number of methods like markers, paint brushes, or brush pens to write text. In digital design, that can take the form of fonts that are designed to emulate the look of fancy, handwritten text.

In every test poster I created, however, ChatGPT seemed to take the phrase “brush lettering” rather literally. Every instance I encountered of a design brief that mentioned any kind of “brush” text generated an image with letters that looked as though they were created with a broad paint brush. A human designer would understand “brush lettering” to mean “something that looks handwritten," but ChatGPT didn’t seem capable of understanding the phrase as anything other than using an actual paint brush.

The generated posters aren’t even using a “font,” strictly speaking. (Often, letters that should be identical had slight variations.) The image generator part of the chatbot is still a diffusion model, so it can’t employ a vector-based font, per se. But the brush-style font is so common that its look surfaces in any statistical model.

This is an odd quirk of ChatGPT specifically, and it’s possible that it could change in the future. Especially if OpenAI intentionally tries to train this behavior out of its chatbot. However, it’s helpful to illustrate the underlying mechanism. The only way a chatbot can conceptualize design elements in a visual medium is to generate more specific text to feed to the image generator. And that text is just as prone to mistakes and blandness as any other AI model.

I’ve been examining this with a focus on the kinds of posters ChatGPT generates because they’re very common, but posters (or any AI-generated content) from other models might look different. Every model has its own tendencies. For example, a lot of vibecoded websites are made with Anthropic’s Claude, and you can often tell by the tiny text, buttons with rounded corners, and tile-based layouts.

To a certain extent, this is inevitable. While AI models are very different from humans and do not make “choices” in the same way people do, design elements still have to come from somewhere, and whether human or AI, it’s impossible to make these decisions in a vacuum. Humans will have preferences based on the things they like or emotionally resonate with, and AI models will have tendencies based on what their statistical model determines is the most appropriate output.

That means that an AI model’s “style” is naturally going to change over time. Even if a model improves or makes fewer mistakes, it’s impossible to ever change the fact that all ChatGPT images are made by ChatGPT. Whatever you generate with any particular model will have a lot in common with what everyone else who uses the same tool generates.

#3326. How Sound Design Helps ‘Minotaur’ Get Away with Murder

Editor’s Note: This article contains spoilers for “Minotaur.”

Director Andrey Zvyagintsev has worked with supervising re-recording mixer Andrey Dergachev for 20 years, since the director’s second film, “Banishment.” On each project, including their most recent portrait of a rotten marriage in a rotten world, “Minotaur,” they’ve tried to improve the sound design—using it as a hook that makes the film’s world feel more vital and alive for the audience.

Seriously, spoilers. This is never more true than in the absurdly sad and funny, then suddenly murderous confrontation between cuckolded husband Gleb (Dmitriy Mazurov) and his wife’s lover Anton (Yuriy Zavalnyouk) at the hinge point of “Minotaur.” Related Stories Super Bowl LXI to Play Live on IMAX Screens ‘Cliff Booth’ Star Elizabeth Debicki on Slapping Brad Pitt, ‘The Movie Critic,’ and the Rom-Com Question

Zvyagintsev and Dergachev generally strive to preserve as much authentic production sound from performances as possible. “On my third movie, ‘Elena,’ we recorded the live sound from shooting, and it’s maybe two or three phrases we had to rerecord, but otherwise the whole sound that you hear is fully recorded during the shooting,” Zvyagintsev told IndieWire on an upcoming episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit podcast. “Our main purpose is to keep as much sound from the shooting as possible and not to add anything extra, and it was the same for ‘Minotaur.’”

But for the moment that Gleb attacks Anton, and its aftermath, it was important to Zvyagintsev that the world beyond the apartment start intruding on Gleb — that even though he wants desperately to cover up what he’s done and make sure no one sees or learns about it, we hear dozens of ways in which he isn’t alone. That required a lot of work outside of the studio to record the background noises Zvyagintsev and Dergachev could then layer into the scene.

“We were creating [background] sounds of the kids playing football in the backyard. We would spend the whole day recording the kids, how they’re speaking, the way they’re playing, people passing by on the street,” Zvyagintsev said. They also recorded different sound layers from Gleb’s luxury SUV, which they could deploy to create maximum panic in both Gleb and the audience.

“The car signals, the leaves on the street, the birds — they all pronounced, and [emphasized] something. So we were modulating all those layers that we recorded, and then we combined them to create the atmosphere and to put it all in one place for the scene,” Zvyagintsev said.

There’s atmosphere from outside and from inside, as Zvyagintsev and Dergachev refused to let Gleb have a moment of peace on the soundtrack — until, as with all the cruel jokes of “Minotaur’s” filmmaking, he gets it in the worst way, at the worst possible moment. There’s a terrible silence once he’s struck Anton on the head with his own camera. And then the world comes rushing back in, even louder than before.

“We were trying to create this volume of sounds right after the hit. And then, when Anton is falling, there is this complete silence. And then somewhere far away we hear the car alarm and even more sounds that create this volume. This is what we were looking for,” Zvyagintsev said.

It was important to finesse the sound design of the sequence so as not to overplay it. Zvyagintsev initially wanted to add music to the moment, but had to hold himself back. “It was really tempting,” Zvyagintsev said. “My composer Evgueni Galperine even wrote the music, which we added. But when we saw the result, we realized, and I understood that no, no, it has to be completely silent.”

Silent as the grave, one might say. But it’s the sound design, the modulation between loudness and silence, that makes the moment so horrifying. Zvyagintsev and Dergachev did it by hand, just to make sure of it.

“Minotaur” is now playing in select theaters.

#3325. 10 Mad Magazine Mascot Alfred P. Neuman Quotes To Live By

The humor periodical Mad started off as a comic in 1952, before taking on its more recognizable magazine with 1955's Mad #24. That cover featured a prominent appearance by the caricature of a character who would come to be known as Alfred E. Neuman. A few issues later, on the cover of Mad #30, Alfred took center stage, officially becoming the magazine's figurehead and mascot.

From its inception, issues of Mad included an epigraph, a quote from a historical figure, politician, or celebrity that set the tone. The first time Mad opened with a quote attributed to Alfred E. Neuman was Mad #38. From that point on, Alfred has had the first, and definitive, line in practically every issue of the magazine since.

Sometimes Alfred's quotes are bawdy, and sometimes they are politically charged. Often, though, they are low-key life lessons, the kind of wisdom that only a comic character can get away with sharing.

"It's a good idea to keep your words soft and sweet because you never know when you'll have to eat them!" Here, Alfred E. Neuman riffs on a centuries-old idiom. Be careful what comes out of your mouth, Neuman warns, because if what you say ends up getting shoved back in your face, down your own throat, you might find yourself choking on the tone and the meanings of your words.

It is sensible advice, especially for comedians, but knowing Alfred, and knowing Mad magazine, this is really a "do as I say, not as I do" case of cautionary advice.

"You'll never get rid of a bad temper by losing it!" There's another saying, which is that you can't control your immediate reaction to something, but you can control your reaction to the reaction. If you're prone to getting angry, giving into it is only going to make the problem worse, that's what Alfred E. Neuman is saying here.

It is a slyly clever bit of wordplay. In fact, this bon mot could be remixed into a riddle. "What can you never get rid of by losing it?" "A bad temper!" The cover for this issue, Mad #71, shows Alfred's mug at the center of a dartboard, and with its opening quote at least, the magazine hit the comedic bullseye.

"Learn from the mistakes of others." That is age-old wisdom. But why? That part is usually left unsaid, but leave it to Alfred E. Neuman to say the quiet part loud. It is "'cause you'll never live long enough to make 'em all yourself!"

Before it was a film franchise, National Lampoon was a groundbreaking American humor magazine; these are the greatest covers from its 3-decade history

Life is finite. There's only so much failure and foible the average person can cram into one lifetime. Recognizing and avoiding others' failures isn't about being more likely to succeed in your own endeavors. It is simply a time-saving exercise. Plus, in some cases, those mistakes might have been fatal, and avoiding them is the only way to guarantee a long life full non-lethal errors in judgment.

The art of the one-liner is trickier than people give it credit for. (Just ask Henny Youngman.) In just a few words, the speaker has to set up and execute the punchline, but there is more to it than that. The line has to conjure an image in people's heads. And that image can be vague, or it can be concrete.

Here, it is literally the latter. "Some minds are like concrete," Alfred E. Neuman says in Mad #82, in the sense that they are "all mixed up and permanently set." In other words, some people are defiantly confused. Obstinately misguided. Flat out wrong and unwilling to revise their opinions. Don't be like those people, Alfred suggests. Be willing to admit your wrong.

Long before Gordan Gecko told the world "greed is good" in Wall Street, Alfred E. Neuman gave Mad readers the real truth about cold hard cash. "Sometimes, the best scheme for doubling your money is to fold it in half and stuff it back in your wallet," Neuman declared in Mad #87.

Meaning, get-rich-quick schemes and seemingly lucrative investments are often not all they seemed cracked up to be. Everyone wants to hustle, and maximize their earnings, but sometimes the smart thing to do is just stack paper. Save up. For Alfred, a folded dollar is worth more than one that is tied up in escrow.

The funny thing about Alfred E. Neuman's advice is that he was often both the angel and the devil on readers' shoulders. His line in Mad #145 exemplifies this. "Sometimes it pays to resist a temptation," he begins. Sounds totally reasonable, and also morally sound, right?

Well, let him finish. Because Alfred also answers why it pays. Not because having will power and self-control are important. Not because resisting temptation is the right thing. No, because temptation is a gamble. Why take the one in front of you when "a better one may be coming along." This hilariously, and cheekily, takes the matter from an ethical equation to a practical matter of when it is the right time to do the wrong thing.

"Experience is something you never have until just after you need it!" This quote from Mad #204 is the perfect companion to the issue's cover, which parodies the Jaws 2 poster, with Alfred E. Neuman piloting a mechanical shark to sneak up on a jet-skiing girl in a bikini.

In the movie, only Chief Brody has the ability to save the day, because only he has the experience of having fought a killer great white before. For most people, most of the time, the toughest moments of their lives are trial and error, giving them the experience that would have made it easier on them only after the fact.

This quote from Mad #221 evokes the earlier entry on this list from Mad #54. It is another way for Alfred E. Neuman to remind readers: "Watch what you say." Especially if you've already gotten yourself in trouble by talking too much.

"When you're in deep water, it's a good idea to keep your mouth shut!" It is a great case of applying a literal lesson to figurative language. If you're in proverbial deep water, or hot water, or any kind of water, talking, or shouting, is only going to result in one thing. Drowning.

Mad #267's cover features a Top Gun parody, and Alfred E. Neuman's quote in the issue makes it clear what kind of people he'd like to strap to the nose of a fighter jet and send flying. "People on ego trips," who, Alfred says bluntly, "should buy one-way tickets."

It is a slick play on words, but the point doesn't mince any. If you are ego-driven and willing to do whatever it takes to feed your own sense of self, take a hike. Take a vacation. Take off and don't come back. For Mad fans, it is a reminder to check themselves before they wreck themselves, and ruin someone else's day too.

The theme of Mad #293's Alfred E. Neuman quote is the same as the prior entry. And it contains essentially the same valuable life lesson. Which is, life is hard for everyone, so don't go around making it harder.

Or as Alfred puts it: "It's not just the ups and downs that make life difficult. It's the jerks." People who go around being miserable all the time need to do more than just sit down and read a Mad magazine, or a Far Side comic, or even a Garfield, and try to lighten up. They need to think about how they are impacting other people. That's what Mad's irreverent, but often on-point mascot is saying here.

#3324. 'Percy Jackson and the Olympians' Season 4 Fate Revealed Ahead of Season 3 Finale

Since joining the team in 2024, she has written more than 1,000 news stories, with her work also cited by outlets like AOL and IMDb.

Three days ago, Disney+'s beloved fantasy series returned for its third season, earning critics' approval with a perfect 100% score on Rotten Tomatoes. Premiering about ten months after the epic Season 2 finale, Percy Jackson and the Olympians Season 3 is expected to conclude on December 11, following its predecessors with an eight-episode run. The new season has not only won over critics but also brought the show back into the spotlight, as it now dominates streaming charts globally. This, of course, includes the U.S., where it has ranked among the top five over the past 48 hours.

While Season 3 is only two episodes in, a fan-favourite star seems to have hinted at the fate of Percy Jackson and the Olympians Season 4. In the meantime, as fans know, that wouldn't be unusual: Season 2 of the Disney+ adaptation wasn't announced until February 2024, after Season 1 ended in late January. Season 3, however, was announced earlier, in March 2025, months before Season 2 premiered that December.

During a recent interview at the Empire State Building about Season 3 of Percy Jackson & the Olympians, Walker Scobell discussed the Greek mythology show's future. Scobell, who has played the titular character since the show began, hinted that there will be a Season 4, saying:

"Let's say we don't get another season. I'm just going to binge all of Percy just to watch it. But since, like, I know we're coming back next season, I can't."

Created by Rick Riordan and Jonathan E. Steinberg, Percy Jackson and the Olympians is based on Riordan's bestselling book series, which began with The Lightning Thief in 2005. Three seasons in, Riordan remains optimistic that the adventure series adaptation will continue, and he previously shared this optimism, noting that Season 2 wasn't greenlit early either. According to the author, while some people are panicking over the lack of a Season 4 announcement, the future remains uncertain.

“We've never finished a season with, like, a guaranteed coming back. But at the same time, it's kind of like ... it would be weird to not come back. It would be weird to not complete this.”

Percy Jackson and the Olympians Season 3 adapts the third book, The Titan's Curse, as the titular demigod returns with his friends for a dangerous quest to rescue his demigod friend Annabeth Chase (Leah Sava Jeffries) and the Greek goddess Artemis (Dafne Keen, who joined in Season 3), both kidnapped by Kronos's army. The fantasy drama also stars Aryan Simhadri, Charlie Bushnell, Nick Boraine, and Jason Mantzoukas, along with Levi Chrisopulos and Holt McCallany, who also joined in Season 3.

Percy Jackson and the Olympians streams on Disney+ and Hulu.

#3323. The Out-of-Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: Looksmaxxing With Dangerous Drugs

A weekly deep dive into the current trends, slang, and viral videos of youth culture in terms that even the squarest can understand.

This week's column is bleak. First, there's the looksmaxxing trend where teenagers are taking dangerous chemicals to correct perceived physical shortcomings. Then there are the AI job interviewers. Depressing, but at least some young people are having a little fun with their dystopian hellscape.

You can judge a generation by the illegal drugs it pioneers. In the 1960s, hippies smoked weed and dropped acid to expand their consciousness; the yuppies of the go-go '80s fueled their drive to acquire with Colombian cocaine; but kids today don’t want to go deeper or work harder. They have a smaller, sadder goal: They take drugs to look better. The substance of choice for a growing number of teenage boys are steroids, peptides, and other exotic chemicals designed to enhance appearance.

Would-be muscle-men have been injecting themselves with black market ‘rhoids since the Eisenhower administration, but that was a small cult of adult weirdos with a specific goal. In 2026, kids are into it, and they aren’t using steroids to win a $500 prize in the Mr. Topeka contest; they’re using unapproved research chemicals to looksmaxx. Looksmaxxing is an online movement of young men trying to maximize their physical appearance. Teenagers are taking the normal desire to look their best to dangerous, pathological levels. Driven by a combination of undiagnosed body dysmorphia and relentless social media algorithms that turn amoral “red pill” kooks into gurus, teenage boys are ingesting a panoply of exotic and dangerous compounds in a quest to fix the angle of their jawlines, change their skin tone, lose weight, grow taller, and otherwise “correct” perceived physical problems.

In the "good old days" of steroid abuse, people generally stuck to abusing anabolic-androgenic steroids that had at least been tested for decades. Teens today are buying SARMs (Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators) and synthetic peptides marked "not for human consumption" from shady laboratories online. Steroids primarily affect the muscles, but many of these newer substances target different biological systems. A recent Rolling Stone article reports that kids are “heightmaxxing” by swallowing erdafitinib, a drug that treats advanced urothelial cancer, because the drug is known to trigger growth spurts (that can result in a curvature of the spine and other nasty side effects). They’re also trying MK-677 to get taller, an experimental growth hormone secretagogue that carries the risk of insulin resistance, water retention, and high blood pressure. Others are injecting Melanotan II, a synthetic peptide that forces a long-lasting deep tan, with side effects of extreme nausea and the sudden, aggressive darkening of moles. (And they're doing steroids too.)

In the looksmaxxing community, softmaxxing is doing generally-considered-acceptable things to look better, like getting enough sleep, exercising regularly, and eating a balanced diet. Hardmaxxing is taking more extreme measures like plastic surgery, smashing your face with a hammer, or taking experimental drugs.

In the bodybuilding and looksmaxxing community, “natty” refers to a natural, non-steroid-enhanced physique.

Here's something more lighthearted than the growing popularity of illicit self-esteem chemicals: the bicep heart and waist heart trends. The Bicep heart came first. Thirst trap videos started appearing on Instagram and TikTok in October in which dudes make a heart with their hand and bicep. Then people started posting variations where they frame the shot with someone they love inside the heart. The bicep heart quickly led to women posting the waist heart.

Okay. So maybe it's not that lighthearted of a trend. While there are some videos of dudes with skinny arms doing the bicep heart, it's mostly jacked dudes. And the waist heart doesn't seem like it would work at all unless you are a specific shape, as this video illustrates. So maybe this isn't a silly meme but an illustration of how young people are inundated with content that can trigger feelings of physical unworthiness, even if they're just looking for silly memes.

As if searching for a job wasn't alienating and horrible enough, some companies have begun using AI agents to conduct interviews. Begging a robot to let you work in a cubicle farm is as dystopian as anything Phillip K. Dick ever imagined, but don't count humanity out yet. Young people are sticking a finger in the eye of the machine by creating comedy videos that focus on trolling these AI job interviewers. They're hilarious because AI is the ultimate straight person in a comedy team, and the raw compute costs to run these interviews means corporate money is burning with each second of wasted time. Here are some of the top creators in the genre.

Bo Bongo: This YouTuber shows up to AI interviews shirtless but insists he's wearing a "corporate tube top," then focuses on daring the interviewer to notice he's doing things like smoking a cigarette or eating a rotisserie chicken.

Cam Whitt likes to wind up AI by arguing, interrupting, telling outrageous lies, and asking the dumbest questions imaginable, like, "When does the interview actually start?" and "How do I figure out what my name is?"

Grahamn Raabe: Among this YouTuber's schticks is speaking only in nonsense, like describing his professional background as "freight cadence, walnut, a little bit of Richard, spruce wood—six years of spruce wood."

Nick Reid: Is so obnoxious, he seems to make the AI furious at him, even though it's a computer without emotions. Two thumbs up!

#3322. From ‘Disclosure Day’ to ‘Devil Wears Prada’: Emily Blunt Breaks Down 10 of Her Greatest Movie Moments

Jimmy Stewart once said that with movies, it’s key moments that people remember.

Emily Blunt, who’s on the circuit these days talking about her standout role as a language-spouting meteorologist in Steven Spielberg’s “Disclosure Day,” gave me some memorable scenes that she will never forget from her wide-ranging filmography. (We spoke on Zoom.)

Clearly, Blunt can deliver in any genre: romance, comedy, musical, sci-fi, action, thriller, drama. So far, Blunt has notched one Oscar nomination, for Supporting Actress in Christopher Nolan’s bio-drama “Oppenheimer.” Sci-fi thriller “Disclosure Day” could score Blunt’s first Best Actress nod. (More below.) Related Stories How Sound Design Helps ‘Minotaur’ Get Away with Murder Super Bowl LXI to Play Live on IMAX Screens

1. “My Summer of Love” (2005, Pawel Pawlikowski) was Blunt’s first movie role. “I remember the wildness of that Edith Piaf dance [‘La Foule’], where I have the cigarette dangling out of my mouth, and she’s trying to romanticize this girl from the wrong side of town and sophisticate her. I remember the scene with Paddy Considine where she tries to seduce him and then she laughs at him. I will never forget the energy in that room and how Paddy was in that scene. I have taken what Pawel taught me about ambiguity and reality on camera, and I have used it throughout my career. I am an untrained actor. I don’t have anything technical to fall back on, but the aliveness that he created on ‘My Summer of Love’ was informative for how I moved forward: what lies beneath the character. You know what the front foot is, and what is the shadow of that person? What’s really going on?”

2. “The Devil Wears Prada“ (2006, David Frankel) marked Blunt’s Hollywood breakout as Miranda Priestley’s beleaguered first assistant Emily Charlton. After she gets hit by a taxi, second assistant Andy Sachs (Anne Hathaway) visits her hospital room. Charlton is angry and tearful at everything she is missing. “The hospital scene makes me laugh because that’s really who she is: this completely broken down, vulnerable, insecure person.”

3. “The Young Victoria” (2010, Jean-Marc Vallée) gave Blunt a queen to embody. “I remember the scene where she asks [Prince] Albert to marry her, because he was not allowed to ask her. She is the monarch, and had to be the one to ask. That scene was so vulnerable and beautifully twinkly, how Jean-Marc shot that.”

4. “The Adjustment Bureau,” a romantic sci-fi thriller, co-starred Matt Damon. “I remember never being able to get through a scene with Matt Damon without laughing. But I did love the scene in the bathroom where they meet. That scene had to sparkle because otherwise you don’t care about them, and you don’t care about them using their magical fedoras to get back to each other. Matt Damon doesn’t know how to be bad. That’s the truth. He doesn’t know how to play a false note. There is something about what Matt does, and he’s so dexterous in his humanity, but I don’t feel it’s technical with Matt. He’s like a laser beam of truth, and I feel myself, anyone who watches him, they ease back and they go, ‘Oh, thank God, Matt Damon’s here.’ He just leads with the truth. He’s like Josh Brolin. They only know how to be honest, and so they have such humanity to them. That’s why you can’t take your eyes off them. John [Krasinski] and I were so proud of what Matt did [with “The Odyssey”]. It’s obviously the most Herculean undertaking, but he grounded everything with that performance.”

5. “Edge of Tomorrow” (2014, Doug Liman) co-starred Tom Cruise and thrust Blunt into action mode for the first time. Her moment was a war scene set on a beach. “It was the beach set, and we started calling it ‘the bitch’ because it was such a nightmare. That set was always flooded. You were always exposed to terrible elements of the weather, freezing, and we shot that beach scene for a month. Tom Cruise gave me a lot of flowers on that one. He was so good to me, and he revealed halfway through the shoot that this was the deep end of action for him— this was the most challenging action movie that he had ever done, and it was my first action movie, so I was flung in at the deep end of action. But we held each other through that. I loved athletics when I was a kid, and then couldn’t be bothered to work out, and then thought I knew what working out was, and then I realized I didn’t know what working out was until I started training for ‘Edge of Tomorrow,’ and that was a transformational thing to my body. She needed to look lethal, absolutely lethal. And so it helped me a lot, doing all of that physicality.”

6. “Into the Woods” (2014, Rob Marshall), adapted from Stephen Sondheim’s stage musical, boasted a huge ensemble cast; Blunt played the baker’s wife opposite James Corden. “‘Moments in the Woods,’ that big song she has right before she gets squished by the giant. She’s weighing up the duality of life, whether she goes for this poetic interlude in her prosaic life or if she goes back to the prosaic life. That kind of agony that she’s going through in the song was cool. I had I’d never sung in front of anyone before, really, other than one small TV thing years ago. I didn’t even want to audition for it, and Rob Marshall said, ‘Look, I’m not looking for singers who can kind of act. I’m looking for actors who can kind of sing,’ and that was great advice. I said it to my 12-year-old this morning as she went off to her musical audition at school. I said, ‘Don’t worry about the notes; just tell us a story. That’s it. That’s what the song should be, and that’s what will make it sound amazing.'”

7. “Sicario” (2015, Denis Villeneuve) plops Blunt’s straight-arrow FBI agent into a violent Mexican border scenario. “The scene that stands out for me is a spellbinding one, when Benicio del Toro comes to my apartment, and he puts the gun to my face and forces me to sign the contract. It’s right at the end of the movie, and I think that scene holds a special place for me because we were not sure about the scene that was written by Taylor Sheridan. It didn’t feel like it belonged in what we were trying to achieve between the characters. We wanted to change it a little bit. It was an idea that Benicio had. We were racking our brains as to how to finish this scene and this moment between the two characters. He always has so many crazy ideas, and he will have some absolute bangers in there. And he called me at about 11 o’clock the night before, and he goes, ‘I think I have it. What about this?’ And I said, ‘That is a great idea, because you’ve got this very idealistic FBI agent who’s pulled into this incoherent, amoral world. And she’s being forced to sign a contract that says everything they did was aboveboard, and that’s like a death to a character like that.’ We rehearsed that scene for two hours. Denis loved it, and then we all turned to [cinematographer] Roger Deakins: “Roger, what do you think?” And he gave his slow nod of approval, and then we shot it, and it was so.”

8. “A Quiet Place” (2018, John Krasinski) was Blunt’s first experience being directed by her husband. The memorable moment: giving birth in the bathtub as a killer monster hovers nearby, listening for any noise. “We shot that whole sequence from the water breaking in the bathtub in order, which I was grateful to John for. It took four days. We did two takes of that bathtub scene because he shot it mainly as a oner. It starts as the blood’s trickling out, and it comes up, and you see the creature, and then it goes into that scream, and then the fireworks go off, but yeah, it’s a wild scene. It’s really smart to have a baby in a silent world. Every woman I’ve spoken to about that scene, they go: ‘Oh my God, that scene made me cross my legs.” And I was: ‘Okay, all right.'”

9. “Oppenheimer” (2023, Christopher Nolan) offered Blunt a constrained role as Kitty, the recessive wife of the great physicist (Cillian Murphy). Blunt agreed that the scene that earned her the Oscar nomination was in the courtroom where she is badgered by the formidable Jason Clarke. “I knew that was the monster scene. When I read the script, I thought, ‘What an extraordinary scene, that you have this person staggering in, looking like a liability,’ and Chris had written that she almost chokes, and you think she’s going to blow it. When I talked to him about it after I read the script, I said, ‘What a reclamation that scene is of that extraordinary brain coming back to life.’ The brain that had gone crazy at the ironing board, probably meant for bigger things than being someone’s wife and someone’s mummy, and I had a great deal of empathy for her and a lot of women who went crazy at the ironing board. She owns Jason Clarke in a way, and you realize she could probably run circles around him. He played such a wonderful bully in that film, but we saw what Meryl [Streep] did with Miranda Priestley: There’s such power in quiet, great, great power and great dignity.”

10. “The Devil Wears Prada 2” (2026, David Frankel) allowed Blunt to indulge Charlton’s excesses. “We all had scenery stuck in our teeth on that one. It was so fun to go back to playing that lunatic. My favorite scene was the funeral scene where she comes in and rants about Dolce and Gabbana. It was such a ludicrous outfit to be wearing to a funeral. Anne Hathaway is the most unstoppable force. And what a wide range of roles she has access to. I feel this moment in her life. She’s in this full wingspan of being able to harness everything she can do and everything she has to offer, and I can’t believe she had the year she just did, and she was pregnant!”

“Disclosure Day” (2026, Steven Spielberg) leaned on Blunt to carry the sci-fi thriller. “The four-and a-half minute oner in the beginning when she arrives at the news station. I’ve seen what Steven Spielberg can do visually, his visual prowess is rather unparalleled. So to be in a oner that he conjures up on the day, that happened spontaneously — he was planning on covering it. And I said, ‘what would help me so much is if you could let me whirlwind out of control in one take from the moment I pull up, going into the makeup room, coming out speaking Korean, she’s in this incoherent tailspin, and then you see her disintegrate over the course of it. And she gets up there to deliver the weather, and she starts to speak in the alien language. Can we just try it as a oner, just for me to see where I’ve got to get to?’ And he watched me do it. And by the time I got up there to do the weather, my legs were shaking. I was out of breath, beside myself, and he loved it. And he goes, ‘We’re going to do it as a oner.’ And we were done by 2 pm. because he planned to shoot it all day. It was Steven in his element of going, ‘Oh, I see it’ and not only was he intentional about creating the environment for me to be able to do that so he didn’t overcover it, he saw a cinematic advantage.”

Blunt plays several characters in one. “All the stuff in the childhood home was deeply moving because that also dealt with that moment where the character goes from crisis to serenity and the ability to then deploy these powers rather than be puppeteered by them. So I loved that shape-shift in the character, like playing two people throughout the course of this film. And the other moment that felt so human to me was the panic attack in the box car after the train sequence, and she’s at max capacity, bubbling over, overwhelmed, and a few people, including myself on set, had experienced panic attacks, and that felt like a real reaction to someone who was utterly overwhelmed. That also felt so Spielbergian: no one’s a slick elite action hero in Steven’s films. Everyone’s afraid. Everyone, including Indiana Jones, everyone’s scared. That hand that’s shaking on the way to Omaha Beach, that is trauma. He can relate to your vulnerabilities. Everyone’s a bit over their head, and in a different action movie, me and Josh O’Connor would have dropped in the boxcar and gone, ‘Whoa, that was crazy.’ And instead, she has a panic attack. I got them a lot in my early twenties, and Steven’s not immune, neither is Josh. All of us have experienced that. That moment where he takes my hands and he puts them on the piano and he goes, ‘This is real. This is real. Feel this. I’m here. You’re here. We’re here.’ I’ve done that. So it just was like, ‘Oh my God!’ You get to sublimate what you’ve experienced into this creative art form sometimes. That’s the great gift often on movies.”

The languages were right in Blunt’s wheelhouse. She has always loved languages. She learned them two to three months before the start of the shoot. “I learned those scenes. The first thing I learned was the Russian and the Korean, because I wanted it to be spoken at such a velocity that it sounded as conversational as it does as me speaking to you right now, and she doesn’t know she’s speaking Russian,” she said. “She thinks she’s speaking English. You have someone who is white-knuckling their way through most of this film, and these forms of mind control are unconscious to her in the beginning, it’s compulsive.”

Next up: “Walk the Blue Fields” directed by John Crowley and co-starring Andrew Scott as another hot priest, Father Joe, presiding at a wedding. “It’s a short story that I bought the rights to about six years ago by Claire Keegan. If you’ve ever read any of her short stories, they’re like laser beams. They’re so wonderful. My sister Felicity is a book agent. She represents Claire, and she sent it to me. Story A is a wedding day, and story B is what led up to that wedding and why everything is starting to unravel on the wedding day. And it plays like a thriller,” she said. “She’s coming back to Ireland to try to build a relationship with her Irish father [Ciaran Hinds] after they’ve been estranged for years, and it’s a story about identity and religion and love. Andrew Scott has to be one of the most beautiful actors I’ve ever shared a scene with.”

And, of course, John Krasinski’s upcoming “Quiet Place 3,” which co-stars Jack O’Connell, Cillian Murphy, Jason Clarke and Noah Jupe, is shrouded in secrecy. “I don’t want to blow John’s cover here,” she said. And “Sicario 3” is also moving forward with the original cast, a script by James Bond writer Steven Knight and director Padraic McKinley.

#3319. Netflix's 8-Part Hard Sci-Fi Series Is Already Renewed For 2 More Seasons

While there are a lot of great original sci-fi shows to come out of Netflix over the years, only one has preemptively avoided a major industry issue with its two-season renewal. It’s a tale as old as time. Viewers are only just getting into a new series, often an ambitious genre show with sci-fi, fantasy, or horror elements, when it is abruptly canceled despite critical acclaim.

From HBO’s one-season wonder Lovecraft Country to the iconic space western Firefly, there is no shortage of promising shows that were unexpectedly ended early by shock cancellations. Often, this leaves their storylines frustratingly unfinished, and fans end up feeling short-changed no matter how much money might have been spent on the budget of these shows during their runs. One need only look at Prime Video’s fantasy series The Wheel of Time for another example.

While the Robert Jordan adaptation was consistently critically adored throughout its three-season run, the show’s abrupt ending arrived long before the series had adapted the entire literary saga to the small screen. As such, what had felt like three increasingly promising seasons of fantasy TV ended up seeming instead like a lot of buildups to nothing. This is why it is so exciting to hear that Netflix’s 3 Body Problem has already avoided this issue with a preemptive two-season renewal.

Based on Chinese novelist Liu Cixin’s trilogy of books Remembrance of Earth's Past, 3 Body Problem’s title came from a real-life Newtonian physics problem. Fittingly enough, 3 Body Problem’s plot focused on a group of scientific researchers from different disciplines, dubbed the “Oxford Five,” coming together to investigate the mysterious deaths of their fellow academics. Eventually, the group unmask a secret conspiracy involving a cult and alien fleets that are preparing to invade earth.

Only, that’s not quite an accurate summary, since 3 Body Problem’s depiction of first contact with extraterrestrial life isn’t as simple as invasions or attacks. Unlike the earlier underrated TNT sci-fi series Falling Skies, 3 Body Problem’s extraterrestrials aren’t straightforward sentient, corporeal creatures, and their plans for earth aren’t as obvious as world domination or the intentional, malicious destruction of human civilization.

Instead, 3 Body Problem’s story merges the past, the present, virtual realities, and layered versions of its story told from different perspectives to create a rich, complex character-driven saga. 3 Body Problem is undoubtedly an odyssey, mixing the ambitious scope of earlier genre shows like The Walking Dead, The Expanse, or Game of Thrones with the narrative complexity of Westworld or Lost.

Despite this ambition, 3 Body Problem doesn’t end up overextending itself in its first outing, and the show is now guaranteed to make it to the end of its source story without needing to rush through the plot at a rate of knots. Where earlier Netflix sci-fi shows like Stranger Things expanded their once-modest stories to become ever more commodious and elaborate, 3 Body Problem was always a complicated show.

Luckily, however, Netflix renewed 3 Body Problem for seasons 2 and 3, ensuring the show has sufficient screen time to adapt the remainder of the source novel series. This is particularly reassuring for fans of Remembrance of Earth's Past since, while the novel was celebrated at the time of its release, Liu Cixin’s books were also thought to be unfilmable due to their unique structure.

3 Body Problem needed to reorder events and rejig characters, while still maintaining the same central plot, and pulled this off with aplomb in season 1. However, it is only since Netflix’s renewal that viewers can be reassured 3 Body Problem will be able to stick the show's landing.

#3318. 10 Saddest Deaths in 'Sunrise on the Reaping,' Ranked

Spoiler Alert: This list contains spoilers for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.The Hunger Games has never been shy about putting its characters through absolute misery, and Sunrise on the Reaping is no exception. Set during the 50th year of the Games—its Second Quarter Quell—the latest chapter in Suzanne Collins' dystopian saga follows a young Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada) as he's thrown into an arena designed to be twice as deadly as the usual Games, with 48 tributes fighting for survival.

But as brutal as the competition itself is, it's the people Haymitch loses along the way that make this story truly one of the most devastating additions to the franchise. From friendships forged in the arena to the loved ones left behind in District 12, Sunrise on the Reaping is filled with so many deaths that have left a mark on the young tribute as well as audiences alike. So, here are some of the most poignant ones.

Panache Barker (Jhaleil Swaby) is one of the District 1 Career tributes who enters the Quarter Quell with a clear advantage over many of the other participants. Having already trained since young, he quickly established himself as a dangerous threat, with his arrogance, brute strength, and aggression already creating conflict before the games even began. But Panache's confidence ultimately proves to be his downfall in the arena, as Maysilee Donner (Mckenna Grace) uses her poisoned darts to stealthily kill him, right as he's about to deliver a fatal attack on Haymitch.

Having built himself up as the ruthless antagonist of the games, Panache's sudden takedown isn't particularly heartbreaking on its own. In fact, it initially feels like a moment of relief and dark irony, since he was, after all, constantly brutalizing the other tributes—and seemingly enjoying it. However, despite his actions, there remains an underlying tragedy as Panache is simply just another teenager who was manipulated by the Capitol into becoming a cruel killer. A mere cog in the endless machine.

As another District 1 Career, Silka Sharp (Laura Marcus) was undoubtedly ruthless and skilled—so much so that she became one of the last tributes standing in the arena alongside Haymitch. Their final confrontation is a tense battle that leaves Haymitch badly wounded, and Silka seemingly having the upper hand. But when she corners him towards the area's edge, Haymitch uses the hidden force field to his advantage, taunting her to throw her axe and have the weapon rebound to fatally strike her.

Similar to Panache, Silka's death isn't necessarily upsetting, as it's staged as a pure, triumphant "outsmarting the villain" climax. That's what happens when she's consistently positioned as a lethal powerhouse who's actively gunning to spill blood and win. But she, too, is a tragic product of the Capitol's cruel system. Unfortunately, the movie omits an important book moment of vulnerability that showcased this (yes, we're talking about the chocolate scene).

Wellie (Rada Rae) is one of the Newcomers from District 6, and as one of the youngest competitors in the arena, it's understandable why Haymitch was quick to care for her before the games began. We see this as he offers Wellie his lunch during one of the tribute's meal sessions. Unfortunately, we don't get much from her after that, as her death occurs off-screen with Haymitch finding her body after Silka rings Wellie's bicycle bell as a means to lure him into an ambush.

While the discovery is obviously grim and heartbreaking, audiences who haven't read the book have very little time to get attached to Wellie before she dies. In fact, the film effectively glosses over the important bond forged between Haymitch and Wellie in the game. They even soften her actual death—which was arguably the most gruesome and brutal one of all. Nevertheless, her death still remains an emotional gut punch as she symbolizes the tragic loss of innocents.

Entering the Second Quarter Quell alongside his other District 12 tributes, Wyatt Callow (Ben Wang) quickly becomes a sympathetic figure. Despite the initial hostility surrounding his family's role as oddsmakers—people who took bets on the Hunger Games—Wyatt earns the trust of his fellow tributes and proves that he's willing to protect those who are more vulnerable than himself. Of course, we see this right at the start of the games, during the chaotic Cornucopia bloodbath, as he steps in front of Silka's axe-throw to shield young Lou Lou (Iona Bell).

In this case, his death is truly upsetting because it comes from an act of kindness and sacrifice rather than selfishness or ambition. Wyatt isn't trying to win at someone else's expense. He simply wants to protect Lou Lou, a girl who has already been subjected to the Capitol's cruel manipulation. His willingness to put himself in harm's way makes him an easy character to root for, and his death only reinforces how little room the Games leave for such compassion.

Lou Lou is a tragic figure from the moment she is introduced, as she's essentially sent in as a mere body-double since the Capitol had to cover up the accidental death of Louella McCoy (Molly McCann). Seemingly drugged (or at least conditioned) into playing a role she doesn't fully understand, the girl is thrust into the Games without any control over her own circumstances. Despite surviving the initial bloodbath, she meets her end when she inhales poisonous pollen from the deadly plants scattered throughout the arena.

Naturally, what makes Lou Lou's death so tragic is the sheer indignity of her existence in the Games. For one, her fate was immediately set as she was sent in as a sacrificial pawn—one who doesn't even get to die under her real name. The books at least give hints about her past, but they also reinforce the disturbing lengths the Capitol is willing to go to in order to maintain the illusion of its spectacle. Lou Lou is one of the many victims of a system that sees children as disposable, and her fate is a reminder that the cruelty of the Games extends far beyond the arena's physical dangers.

The tragedy of Louella McCoy is how her death happens before she even gets the chance to enter the arena. During the tribute parade, the horses pulling the chariots are spooked by objects thrown onto the track, causing them to panic and crash. Haymitch is thrown off, while Louella is sadly left trapped in the District 12 chariot, which flips over and drags her across the path. It's brutal to watch and utterly shocking, especially since it sets the stage for Haymitch to boil with anger and openly defy President Snow (Ralph Fiennes).

Incredibly young and never even given the opportunity to fight for her own life, Louella is killed by the very spectacle that the Capitol insists is meant to honor them. If anything, it exposes just how careless and cruel the system (and its people) truly are, particularly since they flippantly replace her with another girl the next day. By erasing her loss, the Capitol once again strips a child of their dignity, just for the sake of maintaining the illusion of control.

Despite her sharp-tongued nature, Maysilee Donner grows to become one of Haymitch's closest allies as they fight to protect each other across the area. But as the number of tributes begins to dwindle, the two consciously decide to go their separate ways as neither wants to watch the other die (or be responsible for it). Moments later, a cannon fires, and they rush back towards each other, only for a flock of bird mutts to fatally attack Maysilee, with Haymitch scrambling to protect her in his arms.

Of course, the moment is agonizing to watch as Maysilee isn't just another tribute Haymitch loses along the way. She's a slice of home and a true friend who shares his determination to survive without surrendering completely to the brutality of the Capitol. Yes, there are significant changes from the book that shape her death as collateral punishment for Haymitch rather than a direct consequence of her own acts of rebellion. However, the stellar performance between Zada and Grace makes up for this omission, with their chemistry carrying the emotional weight of a relationship built on genuine care and humanity—even as they're in a competition designed to strip its participants of precisely that.

As the son of the legendary victor, Beetee (Kelvin Harrison Jr.), Ampert Latier (Percy Daggs IV) is a clever and resourceful young boy who helps recruit Haymitch to sabotage the Games as a means to undermine the Capitol's control. Their plan succeeds in disrupting the system, but the Capitol retaliates by unleashing vicious squirrel mutts on Ampert. Haymitch finds him being attacked and desperately tries to intervene. Sadly, the creatures horrifically overwhelm the young tribute, leaving Haymitch unable to save him.

Ampert's death is particularly tragic because he symbolizes the devastating risks of daring to challenge an authoritarian regime. Like some others, the young boy's fate of death was already sealed thanks to his father's prior acts of rebellion. As a result, his courage and willingness to risk everything for a chance at freedom only makes his loss all the more shattering—especially since it happens in such a brutal manner (one that's even worse and more gruesome in the books).

After unexpectedly surviving the Second Quarter Quell and returning to District 12 as a victor, Haymitch is confronted with the consequences of his defiance: his home is engulfed in flames where both his mother (Kara Tointon) and little brother, Sid (Smylie Bradwell), were trapped inside. Of course, it's clear that President Snow has made good on his threats, with Haymitch having nothing to do but watch as his entire family is taken from him. To make matters worse, the tragedy becomes even more painful when they reveal that mother and son were found holding onto each other, resulting in them being buried in the same casket.

There's something especially cruel about this punishment, as Haymitch's family are true innocents. Neither knew of his plans, and yet they were forced to pay the price. In this sense, Snow isn't merely trying to silence a rebellious victor. He's making an example of Haymitch and ensuring that his victory comes with a lifetime of suffering. The loss of Ma and Sid also strips Haymitch of the very support system he desperately needs after the Games, leaving him isolated and increasingly broken. It's a deeply personal act of vengeance, and one that helps explain why Haymitch eventually retreats into deep despair.

Just when you think Haymitch has lost so much, he's met with another devastating blow. After the funeral of his family and fellow tributes, he finally reunites with his long-love, Lenore Dove Baird (Whitney Peak), who has finally been released from captivity. And for a fleeting moment, their reunion offers a glimmer of hope as she happily pulls out a bag of gumdrops she found on the rocks, thinking them to be a gift. Haymitch, in turn, feeds one to her—only for him to quickly realize that it was a trap planted by Snow. Once again, he's left helpless in his desperation and can do nothing but watch someone he loves die in his arms.

Her death is distressing not just because it's Lenore Dove, but because of what she represents to Haymitch. Throughout the film, she's one of the few people who genuinely understands his anger at the Capitol and even encourages him to believe things can change. She isn't simply a romantic interest, but a person whose conviction and rebellious spirit help shape the person Haymitch becomes. Even as she dies, Lenore Dove makes him promise to keep fighting against the oppressive system, turning her final moments into one last act of defiance. And knowing what Haymitch's emotional journey looks like in the future makes this loss all the more heartbreaking as audiences realize that it's his memories of the people he loved that have kept him going.

#3317. The Best Visual Effects in ‘Wildwood’ Are the Ones You Can’t See — Watch

There are all sorts of magic worlds waiting to be discovered in the stop-motion epic “Wildwood,” but it’s a credit to the film that one of them is Portland, Oregon. Laika Studio’s Head of CG Animation Benoit Dubuc was involved early and often in order to determine what would be shot practically by the stop-motion animation team and what CG effects would be used to achieve. Even in the most mundane and ordinary moments of the film question of either/or. It was one of how the collaboration between different kinds of animation would work.

“We mostly shoot two or three puppets at a time, so any time that there’s background characters, they’re gonna be digital,” Dubuc said during IndieWire’s Craft Roundtable on visual effects. He pointed out that when Baby Mac gets kidnapped by a murder of crows under the command of the dread sorceress Alexandra (Carey Mulligan), the amount of work to achieve that moment fully through stop-motion would mean they’d probably still be animating it. Related Stories From ‘Disclosure Day’ to ‘Devil Wears Prada’: Emily Blunt Breaks Down 10 of Her Greatest Movie Moments How Sound Design Helps ‘Minotaur’ Get Away with Murder

“We’ll often get [animators] to produce some practical work to lead the visual effects work. We built a crow puppet to spec. We didn’t animate it in the film, but it informed the visual effects work. We try to stay away from simulations as much as possible, knowing that what we’re chasing is something that feels handmade and something that is slightly imperfect,” Dubuc said.

That goes for individual characters and for the vibrant backgrounds of “Wildwood” alike. “The audience would think that we built sets the size of an airport hangar with a hundred thousand practical puppets running downhill. It’s not possible,” Dubuc said. The fact that it looks possible, in both the most intricate battle sequences and the ordinary chaos of biking past Powell’s Books, means that the VFX team has done its job. “ The portrayal of Portland that we were striving for is a beautiful, vibrant city,” Dubuc said.

#3316. Halide camera app just got even better for iPhone Duo

Halide 3.4 is out today as the latest update to the pro camera app. The update adds several new features, including a larger viewfinder for iPhone Duo and more.

The new Halide update also lets you use the outer screen on iPhone Duo as a live preview or a fill flash. It brings back a few camera tools from Halide Mark II as well.

Lux Optics first added iPhone Duo support in October with Halide 3.3. With the phone fully open, the initial iPhone Duo update let you review your most recent photo alongside the live viewfinder.

Today’s new XL mode gives you the option to swap the photo preview for a larger viewfinder. Controls on both sides enable two-handed shooting.

While the Duo is open, the outer screen can mirror Halide’s camera controls or show a full-screen viewfinder without controls. The second option lets the person you’re photographing see how you’ve framed the shot.

In low light, Halide can use the outer screen as a fill flash. That gives you a softer source of light for portraits, and Halide’s developers recommend turning the screen brightness all the way up before taking the photo.

Halide also now places the histogram along the Duo’s crease. The update revises the Photo Lab interface for editing with the Duo half open as well.

On other iPhones, Halide 3.4 restores the color and luminance histograms and the shutter timer from Mark II.

Halide Mark III launched back in May with a redesigned camera and the new Photo Lab editor. Recent updates added RAW-only capture in 3.1 and Aperture Priority for iPhone 18 Pro in 3.2. Halide Mark III version 3.4 is available now on the App Store.

#3314. iOS 27 gave AirPods Pro a convenient new setting, here’s how to use it

iOS 27 gave AirPods Pro a variety of new features, but there’s another addition that’s easy to miss: a convenient new setting in Control Center for Adaptive Audio.

Several AirPods models offer excellent Active Noise Cancellation and Transparency modes—especially AirPods Pro 3 (now only $179).

But Adaptive Audio is another option you may or may not have tried. The feature aims to blend the strengths of both ANC and Transparency in a single mode.

And in iOS 27, Apple added a new setting to let you conveniently fine-tune Adaptive Audio to your preferences.

While wearing AirPods, open Control Center on your iPhone and tap the volume slider, then hit ‘Listening Mode’ in the bottom-left corner. Here you’ll see the standard listening mode options.

New in iOS 27 though, when ‘Adaptive’ is selected, you can now use a Liquid Glass slider to adjust whether the mode lets in more or less external noise.

Slide it to the left and Adaptive Audio will more closely resemble Transparency, while sliding it to the right makes it cancel out more noise.

You can also move the new slider incrementally to achieve exactly your ideal balance of Transparency and Noise Cancellation. It’s not limited to just a few preset options.

This Control Center slider is available on all AirPods models that support Adaptive Audio.

Do you ever use Adaptive Audio, and if so, have you adjusted it at all? Let us know in the comments.

#3313. AI Film ‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts’ Deemed Ineligible by Academy for Best Animated Feature Oscar

“Gods Don’t Give Gifts,” an upcoming film from YouTuber Gossip Goblin that was made entirely with generated artificial intelligence, was deemed ineligible for the Best Animated Feature Oscar at the upcoming Academy Awards.

As IndieWire previously reported on “Gods Don’t Give Gifts,” which is the first fully AI movie to be released theatrically, the film had submitted for consideration and had planned FYC screenings alongside its theatrical release on December 4.

But the film was not included among the list of 38 animated films deemed eligible for this year’s Oscars that were announced Monday, November 23. IndieWire understands that the Academy’s Animation Branch Executive Committee determined “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” did not meet the Academy’s definition of an animated film under the rules for the 99th Awards. Related Stories The Best Visual Effects in ‘Wildwood’ Are the Ones You Can’t See — Watch From ‘Disclosure Day’ to ‘Devil Wears Prada’: Emily Blunt Breaks Down 10 of Her Greatest Movie Moments

Here’s the full rule as written that the Academy felt “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” did not satisfy:

An animated film is one in which characters or objects are given the illusion of life by having movement created for them, by any human means. While the crucial movement of a live-action motion picture is captured at speed, animation is the craft of human creation and manipulation of images to produce a performance from inanimate objects. At least 75 percent of the motion picture’s running time, without opening or end credits, must include animation of the primary subject or subjects. An animated feature has a running time of more than 40 minutes. Upon submission, filmmakers must provide information supporting how the motion picture qualifies as an animated film.

Edward Saatchi, a producer on “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” with Fable Studios, told IndieWire he and director Zack London (a.k.a. Gossip Goblin) plan to appeal the animation branch’s decision and cited the example of Richard Linklater’s rotoscoped film “Apollo 10 1/2,” which was originally deemed ineligible but saw the branch reverse its decision upon appeal. Saatchi said that the film, in addition to submitting for Best Animated Feature, also submitted in other categories such as Best Director, Adapted Screenplay, VFX, and Sound. But if the film doesn’t fall under the animation branch today, he believes eventually AI movies will inevitably find a place somewhere within Academy rules, even if it ends up being a theoretical “Best AI Movie” category.

“‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts’ is starting a big debate around where cinematic works of art made with AI fit. Is it time to consider a ‘Best AI Movie?’ Do these films fit best in the voice-actor led animation category? Is AI simply the new VFX? It’s going to take the whole industry time to figure it out,” Saatchi said. “With traditional garlanded directors like Matthieu Kassovitz, Alex Proyas, and Doug Liman making heavily-AI films, it’s going to be a good debate of how to categorize. We think Best Animated is simplest, but it may be the Academy decides ultimately that a Best AI movie category will make the most sense with these films where everything you’re seeing is generative.”

Of note, one of the films that did qualify for Best Animated Feature was “Coyote vs. Acme,” which is a hybrid animated and live-action film featuring the Looney Tunes alongside human actors in the real world. The Academy on Monday also announced the eligible features in the Best Documentary Feature race and the Best International Feature race.

As part of the Academy’s most recent rules changes from earlier this year, only roles credited in the film’s legal billing that are demonstrably performed by humans with their consent are eligible for acting categories, and screenplays must be human-authored to be eligible. That rule changed followed on guidelines from last year ahead of the 98th Oscars in which the Academy specified, “[Gen-AI] tools neither help nor harm the chances of achieving a nomination. The Academy and each branch will judge the achievement, taking into account the degree to which a human was at the heart of the creative authorship when choosing which movie to award.”

In the case of “Gods Don’t Give Gifts,” the film has a script written by London, and though all the characters in the film are generated with AI visually, it features real human actors doing the voice work for the characters. The film also features cameos of some real-life people playing parts resembling themselves, most notably the pop star Grimes. But the film has elaborate look books, visual reference points, and photo mashing that all went into the creation of these characters, something that clearly has human authorship and goes beyond a computer interpreting a single prompt.

Part of Gossip Goblin’s battle in legitimizing “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” is in showing there was a human team, between 30-35 people, working for years on the film’s creation. Gossip Goblin also recently released a behind-the-scenes documentary that showcases the film’s composer, its foley artist, its voice actors, and more detailing the human effort that went into the project.

Discussion over AI in Oscar eligible films came to a head after several movies in the 2024 Oscar race were reported to have included AI in their post-production editing process, including “A Complete Unknown,” “The Brutalist,” and “Emilia Pérez.” The examples were for traditional VFX, not for anything that enhanced or altered performances, but the Academy as a result now requires disclosure of AI if it is used in a film.

“Gods Don’t Give Gifts” begins its theatrical run on December 4, which will initially be an Oscar-qualifying run, and it will expand on January 22 alongside a rollout with the film’s international distributor AGC International.

#3312. 10 Funny Movies To Watch With Your Family This Thanksgiving

Thanksgiving is a time of great football, food, and family. Whether you're gathering with blood relatives or a chosen family, the spirited holiday offers a chance to slow down and reflect on all the things, big and small, to be thankful for. There's nothing better than stuffing yourself with moist turkey, melt-in-your-mouth mashed potatoes, green bean casserole, and freshly baked dinner rolls before camping in front of the TV for a nap (or two) and long-overdue family time with favorite comedies and family-friendly movies.

There are countless holiday movies and TV, including Thanksgiving-themed episodes of The Simpsons, to watch to put you in the mood for gratitude and celebration. Thanksgiving is the perfect time to take time off from work, reconnect with loved ones, and laugh a little.

Millennials will undoubtedly remember Robin Williams' bonkers performance in Les Mayfield's sci-fi comedy Flubber. Through developing a new energy source, Medfield College professor Philip Brainard (Williams) invents a sentient green goo that escapes before flying through the neighborhood. Brainard must recapture it, prove its worth to the college board, and steal back his fiancé, college president Sara Jean Reynolds (Marcia Gay Harden), from his arch nemesis. Slapstick gags and raucous humor characterize this family-friendly gem that has never gotten its proper due.

Williams always dove headfirst into his roles, particularly when it came to comedy. He committed to the bit and delivered knockout performances. As Brainard, he manages to find a tremendous heart pounding at the center of the movie's themes of love and thankfulness.

Director Gurinder Chadha takes cues from National Lampoon's Christmas Vacation, but makes the story a tasty Thanksgiving treat. The family gathers for a tremendous feast, but there's naturally plenty of hijinks from various oddball relatives that would give the Griswold family a run for their money. The cast is as star-studded as they come and includes Kyra Sedgwick, Julianna Margulies, and Alfre Woodard.

The hilarious ensemble piece celebrates dysfunctional families (we all have one) and how to find even the smallest things for which to be thankful. What's Cooking? also shines a spotlight on different kinds of families and relationships. It's not only about blood relatives, but a chosen family comes into view, as well.

The Barry Sonnenfeld-directed and starring comedy, Addams Family Values serves as a sequel to 1991's The Addams Family, but it can be viewed on its own without any prior knowledge of the original. For not-yet-inducted family members, Addams Family Values supplies all the macabre, yet good-natured, humor you could want, including an epic scene of Wednesday (Christina Ricci) lighting the set of a camp play on fire.

Joan Cussack joins the cast as Fester's (Christopher Lloyd) new gold-digging wife Debbie Jellinsky, a black widow with a thirst for killing her husbands. In true Addams Family fashion, Values normalizes the strange with smartly written dialogue and funny bone-tickling physicality. It's a guaranteed laugh fest.

Rewatching A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving has been a Thanksgiving tradition for many families for decades - and for good reason. But for those who haven't experienced it yet, Charlie Brown and his friends' antics deliver both humor and thoughtfulness. It's about honoring the holiday through a melodramatic story about Charlie Brown throwing a feast. Naturally, the shenanigans make it a welcome addition to anyone's festivities. And oh yes, the physical football gag is pure cinema.

A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving reminds us to be thankful for the life we've been given, the people who make it worth living, and how we can find a silver lining when things go wrong. Charlie Brown might get exasperated with his friends, but he loves them and wouldn't trade them for the world.

Decidedly not for kids, Donald Petrie's Grumpy Old Men gears its witty, sometimes vulgar, humor for older audiences. Max (Walter Matthau) and John (Jack Lemmon) hate each other, and they've been fighting since 1938. As they've grown older, they've learned to cherish their friendship, oddly enough. They hold grudges, that's to be sure, and will do anything for a good dose of payback. But when things go sideways, health-wise, it becomes clear that they really do care deeply about one another.

Beneath the humor, Grumpy Old Men contains powerful messages about living every day like one's last, cherishing friendships, letting go, and bracing for the future. Matthau and Lemmon expertly offer up performances that capture the humor and heart of the situation. It's also about allowing others into your world when it's the most difficult mountain to climb.

Robin Williams' turn as Alan Parrish in Joe Johnston's Jumanji never gets old. As a child, he discovers a wooden boardgame buried on the site of his father's factory. He takes it home and begins to play, inviting his crush Sarah Whittle (Laura Bell Bundy) to join him. Well, things end horribly with Alan being sucked into the game for decades. Sarah grows into a woman (now played by Bonnie Hunt) afraid of the world and in therapy.

Two kids, Judy (Kiersten Dunst) and Peter (Bradley Pierce), move into the old Parrish house and find the game. They unwittingly unleash giant killer mosquitoes, mischievous monkeys, and a flesh-hungry lion. Oh, and they also free Alan from the game, along with hunter Van Pelt (Jonathan Hyde), who is on a mission to kill him. Dated CGI aside, Jumanji makes you grateful for the cards you've been dealt in life because it could all be worse. What's more, it's one of the best family-friendly movies of the 1990s.

Planes, Trains, and Automobiles stars John Candy and Steve Martin at the top of their game. When Neal (Martin) and Del (Candy) travel home for Thanksgiving, they get a rude awakening when a snowstorm hits the Midwest that prevents them from landing in Chicago. As such, they end up stranded in Wichita, Kansas, and then travel by train and, you guessed it, automobile just to get home to their families. Wackiness leads to an unlikely friendship that makes the film a holiday essential.

A surprising emotional core emerges by the last scene, boosting the already great film into the stratosphere. Planes, Trains, and Automobiles isn't only about the humor but the real heart.

The Muppets doesn't get talked about enough. The comedy musical features all the usual suspects: Kermit the Frog, Miss Piggy, Fozzie the Bear, Animal, and countless others. After parting ways, everyone went off to live their own lives. Some stepped further into the spotlight, while muppets like Kermit retreated into the shadows. Their once-cherished studio has fallen into a derelict state and is being sold to Tex Richman (Chris Cooper), who plans to demolish the property and drill for oil.

When Gary (Jason Segel) takes his girlfriend Mary (Amy Adams) and muppet brother Walter (Peter Linz) to Hollywood, they make a stop at the rundown Muppets studio only to see how tragic it is now. Walter plots to get the band back together in order to raise $10 million in order to save the property from utter destruction. The Muppets is equal parts road trip movie and flashy musical that knows exactly how to tug on the heartstrings, delivering tearful moments aplenty. Of course, it's also characterized by a signature style and humor that make any day truly joyful.

A loose remake of the 1950 movie of the same name, Shawn Levy's Cheaper by the Dozen examines big families, and there's no better time than Thanksgiving to revisit or watch it for the very first time. Steve Martin and Bonnie Hunt play Tom and Kate Baker, heads of a household to a whopping total of 12 children. When Kate launches her book tour, Tom is left to parent all 12 kids without any guidance or know-how on taking care of so many at once. It's a hilarious premise that more than delivers the laughs.

For all big families out there, Cheaper by the Dozen no doubt resonates with its situational humor, particularly when it comes to siblings fighting and a father that can't handle the heat in the kitchen. Once again, Martin knocks it out of the park with his performance, and the cast, which includes pop star Hilary Duff, rises as one of the best comedic ensembles ever.

Jimmy Hayward's 2013 animated movie Free Birds resets Thanksgiving Day as not Turkey Day but Pizza Day. When a smart turkey named Reggie (Owen Wilson) gets selected as the president's pardoned turkey, he enjoys a lavish life of late-night TV and all the pizza he can eat. But a rogue turkey enlists him, or rather kidnaps him, for a top secret mission, and Reggie goes back in time to stop turkeys from being on the menu for Thanksgiving.

Free Birds stars a smorgasbord of big-name talent, including Amy Poehler, Woody Harrelson, Keith David, George Takei, and Dan Fogler, and makes dozens of wisecracking jokes about the game Angry Birds. At the end of the day, who doesn't love a bunch of animated turkeys running around trying to save all turkeys from being eaten on Thanksgiving?
