#3309. There's Actually a Simple Explanation for All These Widespread Outages

It feels like every time you look at your phone lately, another company is having an outage. Last week, there was Microsoft, whose outage took down services from Outlook to Teams. Then, the FAA grounded all flights across the U.S. following "communication issues." This week, a number of banks experienced outages, as did Apple. Even the NSA's internal communications network went dark. Some of the biggest corporations and organizations in the world can't seem to keep their services running, leading to widespread disruptions and confusion. When it's a one-off, it's an annoyance; when it's outage after outage, it starts to feel like a pattern.

That pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public. What could possibly be causing Apple, Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase, and the NSA alike to go dark at roughly the same time? Is it a coordinated cyberattack? An AI revolt? Is the end finally nigh? To an outside observer, it certainly appears like something coordinated and nefarious is happening here. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is insistent that there is "zero evidence" that hackers or bad actors caused any of these outages, and President Trump is particularly unconcerned by the whole ordeal, saying, "It's life," and "Things like that happen."

But to skeptics of the U.S. government, these trickles of information aren't necessarily reassuring. While I agree with calls for someone from the government (perhaps the president himself) to make an official announcement explaining the situation, the root cause does appear to be clear at this time: The short answer? AI is at fault here, but not in the way you think.

Love it or hate it, AI is a force to be reckoned with. While you might know that AI can generate hyper-realistic videos and manage your emails on your behalf, certain models are adept at discovering new security vulnerabilities in software. These models aren't just helpful tools; they far surpass the abilities of human researchers. You might remember Anthropic initially pulled the brakes on its breakthrough model, Claude Mythos, when it found that the model could root out security vulnerabilities in just about anything.

Mythos, and models like it, are a double-edged sword. On the one hand, they can be major assets for developers and researchers to find new security vulnerabilities that humans otherwise wouldn't have discovered, and patch them accordingly. Unfortunately, the same can be said for bad actors, who can use these models to learn about new security flaws and attempt to exploit them before researchers have a chance to find them. As such, software developers across the spectrum, from small-time devs to major corporations, have been racing to patch as many security vulnerabilities as they can find—and they're finding a lot.

You might notice your PC's security updates, for example, are shipping with more patches than usual—historic levels, even. Microsoft keeps breaking its own records with its Patch Tuesday updates, including over 1,400 fixes with its October update. The company's October 2025 Patch Tuesday update, by comparison, included fewer than 180 fixes.

It's important to understand that just about every company that develops software is furiously working to patch its systems before hackers or AI agents exploit vulnerabilities first. And while there are successes (Microsoft is now protecting its customers from thousands of flaws each month), this speed is also inadvertently breaking things along the way. That's not just speculation: According to The Washington Sun, both Wall Street executives and the NSA explained to members of Congress that patching security flaws discovered by AI models caused this week's widespread outages.

Barring some campaign to cover up a coordinated attack on systems and services, it does seem like these outages are simply the result of companies breaking their own products in an attempt to stop AI-assisted hackers from exploiting undiscovered flaws. But that's not all that reassuring, either. AI models are only going to keep getting better at finding vulnerabilities; likewise, AI agents are only improving at hacking into systems autonomously. Companies will need to ramp up their efforts to patch their software before both hackers and AI agents discover those flaws first, and so the cycle will continue. Unless something changes, we may see routine outages as companies try to fix things as quickly as possible.

The implications aren't specific to any one company, either. Our world increasingly relies on fewer companies to keep us all connected. We saw that last year, when cloud hosting providers like AWS and Cloudflare each experienced outages. When these services go down, so do all of the networks that rely on them. If AWS or Cloudflare break something while trying to patch their systems, whole parts of the internet go dark.

Of course, it'll only be more difficult for the general public—if not the developers themselves—to recognize when outages are the result of maintenance or a cyberattack. Just because recent outages don't appear to be nefarious in nature, that doesn't mean future outages will be so innocent. For the time being, however, it seems we can worry less about an active cybersecurity incident, and more about how AI is disrupting modern life in ways few of us saw coming.

#3308. Why Is the ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Trailer So… Gloomy? Internet Erupts Over Latest Look at Marvel Movie

There’s a storm brewing, chere, and it has nothing to do with the weird Gambit (Channing Tatum) and Herbie the Robot Dunkin Donuts ads that played like once a quarter during all the football games on Sunday.

The final trailer was released ahead of Marvel’s “Avengers: Doomsday,” the mega-Sentinel, crossover-tastic 165-minute Russo Brothers opus out on December 18. And the response hasn’t been great — in part because Cyclops says, “To me, my X-Men!” and there isn’t actually a Storm.

Way back in the salad days of 2012, Joss Whedon first did an “Assemble” shot that roved in a circle all of the original “Avengers” film, while an Alan Silvestri score bwaaamped the brassy “Avengers” theme. Say whatever you like about Whedon’s strengths and weaknesses when it comes to visual style, but the first time this happened, the shot’s continuous nature served a storytelling purpose. It was the cinematic way to finally bind these crazy kids together in superhero fellowship — through the timeless crucible of New York City getting shredded into CGI bits by alien-monster things. Related Stories AI Film ‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts’ Deemed Ineligible by Academy for Best Animated Feature Oscar The Best Visual Effects in ‘Wildwood’ Are the Ones You Can’t See — Watch

But over the many, many Phases of the MCU, the Avengers Assemble shots have kept happening. And happening. And sure enough, the “Doomsday” trailer crescendos with a bunch of our heroes stuck in a gray-black wasteland void that looks like a glitched “Expedition 33” loading screen, with the camera straining to create that same sense of unity.

It doesn’t. At least not in the trailer. Which is why so much of the response to the finale “Doomsday” trailer has been focused on it.

As folks online have pointed out, Steve Rogers (Chris Evans) looks like he’s standing in entirely different lighting from the people closest to him. There’s no sense of texture or proximity that suggests anybody was placed against the same green screen together, let alone acting together (a problem that has been pointed out about the filmmaking process for “Doomsday” already).

No amount of money can make up for shooting for maximum flexibility — which so often can devolve into being indecisive — or for pursuing relentless revisions throughout the VFX pipeline. That is exactly what leads to shadowy, sloppily-framed environments like wherever the hell the Avengers are fighting Doctor Doom (Robert Downey Jr.) and his creations. And because the environment is so flattened and indistinct, only the barest hints of color survive. And really, only because Reed Richards (Pedro Pascal) is still wearing a coat from a different movie.

Now, what comes most naturally to Cyclops is shooting an optic blast from his eyes, and what comes most naturally to us is posting negative takes online. The trailer takes that shot out of context for nostalgia’s sake; its dramatic purpose within the film itself might be more complicated, or the setup for a twist in three different timelines’ worth of Avengers’ fortunes. But when it comes to all the cinematic crimes of artless visuals, repetitive plots, and overbearing lore that have contributed to superhero fatigue? The “Avengers: Doomsday” trailer doesn’t seem to be beating the charges.

#3306. Darkseid Unveils His Justice League, All Members And Powers

The Justice League are DC's greatest heroes - bastions of heroism and self-sacrifice - which makes it all the more disturbing that Darkseid just assembled his own version of the team. His roster combines some shock members with heavyweights designed to counter Batman, Superman and Wonder Woman.

Recent years have seen Darkseid take his rightful place as the overarching villain of all DC canon, as 2024's All In Special saw him leave behind his mortal limits and become a multiversal god, founding the Absolute Universe and spreading his influence out into the multiverse.

The recent DC All In Saga: Darkseid vs. the World #1 (Scott Snyder, Sanford Greene) confirmed that his plans remain on track, as well as revealing that the God of Evil has assembled his own personal Justice League. Here's every member of Darkseid's superhuman army (at least, so far.)

DC All In Saga: Darkseid vs. the World #1 sees Darkseid arrive on Earth-3, the home of the villainous Crime Syndicate. This group is DC's classic evil Justice League, mirroring the heroes of classic canon. Darkseid demands the Syndicate join him as his thralls, only for their leader Ultraman to launch an attack on Darkseid. Of course, he's quickly beaten to a pulp and drafted into the archvillain's service.

An incredibly powerful bully, Ultraman keeps Earth-3 under his thumb despite not being particularly intelligent or creative with his powers. He has the basic abilities of Superman, with the exception that Kryptonite only makes him stronger, leading him to seek out, crush and snort the radioactive rock wherever he finds it.

Ultraman once imprisoned Superman's son in his dimension, taunting and abusing him for years, leading the mainstream Clark Kent to develop a seething hatred of his opposite number. Recently, DC introduced Ultraman and Superwoman's son Ultraboy, though he isn't shown on Earth-3 when Darkseid attacks the Syndicate.

Having arranged the assassination of his mother and father as a child, Owlman used their fortune to take total control of Gotham city, turning it into his personal kingdom. A genius tactician and combatant, Owlman has an army of 'Talon' sidekicks who he considers totally disposable, sacrificing them on a whim.

Owlman chafes under Ultraman's absolute power, engaging in a stunted affair with Superwoman behind his back. Owlman is one of the few denizens of Earth-3 whose counterpart in DC's main continuity is also a villain - a rival to the Court of Owls formerly known as Lincoln March but claiming to be Batman's brother.

Earth-3's Superwoman is essentially a superpowered dominatrix. She's married to Ultraman but carries out a series of affairs to secretly influence the planet's politics, its supervillain rulers and even its heroes.

Despite being an Amazon, Superwoman possesses the power of the mainstream Superman, with the exception of wielding the Lasso of Submission - a length of barbed wire which forces whoever it binds to worship and obey its wielder.

Possessing the powers of the Flash, Johnny Quick is a superspeed serial killer who takes joy in running through normal humans, causing them to explode. Unlike the mainstream Flash, he's not particularly intelligent, and tends to follow the lead of Crime Syndicate member Atomica, who isn't shown as a member of the Syndicate in DC All In Saga: Darkseid vs. the World #1.

There have been multiple versions of the evil Green Lantern in DC lore, and it's unclear which one appears in DC All In Saga: Darkseid vs. the World #1. The most recent was John Stewart's Emerald Knight. A former police officer, Stewart was recruited by the Overlords of Oa as one of their personal enforcers.

As the Emerald Knight, John can summon powerful energy constructs, with his ring persuading him to kill at every opportunity. His vigilante murders estranged him from his daughter, leading to a further surrender of his humanity to the ring.

In contrast, the former Power Ring of Earth-3 wore a ring powered by the demonic Volthoom, which essentially enslaved the wearer and fed on their lifeforce, unleashing monstrous energy constructs when a fight was to its benefit.

The character shown in Darkseid's Justice League is John Stewart but is referred to as Power Ring, raising questions about which version is considered canon in this frequently rebooted reality.

A mysterious figure straight out of Greek mythology, Pandora is a skilled mystic with a range of magical abilities. Despite powerful magic, she prefers to fight by channeling her power through twin handguns, and is a master of modern and traditional weaponry.

Dying at the hands of Doctor Manhattan at the beginning of DC's Rebirth era, Pandora has been resurrected as Darkseid's "harbinger." He has tasked her with traveling across the multiverse, offering his most powerful enemies the chance to join him. Her first stop is the corpse of the beyond-godlike villain Imperiex, who it's suggested she intends to bring back to life.

Pandora believes that Darkseid intends to eventually consume her (and the villains she recruits) to obtain the 'Omega energy' that is powering his ultimate form, but is content to go along with his plans for the present.

The recent Superman Annual 2026: Year One Thousand revealed that Darkseid has embarked on an agreement with Brainiac, working together to limit Superman's power and influence across the multiverse. Brainiac has taken on the task of kidnapping every version of the Legion of Super-Heroes from across every reality.

Brainiac is at the height of his power, with a gigantic body and godlike technology that makes him a multiversal force. Indeed, he's so powerful that Cyborg Superman (aka Hank Henshaw) is acting as his enforcer, with Brainiac tasking him to patrol the future and ensure no new Legion of Super-Heroes ever forms.

Cyborg Superman has all Clark Kent's powers, plus the ability to take control of essentially all forms of machinery. It appears that the pair may soon split off on their own, with Brainiac scheming to use the combined power of the various Legions he's captured to topple both Darkseid AND Superman. For now, however, he remains in Darkseid's alliance.

The awesome conclusion of DC All In Saga: Darkseid vs. the World #1 reveals the full scale of Darkseid's Justice League. While he spends the issue pacifying and capturing the Crime Syndicate, he then reveals that "I have conquered nearly all variants of Earth" across the multiverse.

He ends the issue surrounded by versions of Superman he's captured and stored in tanks, presumably with the same offer he gives the Crime Syndicate - join him or be consumed as a power source.

While it's not known exactly which versions of Superman Darkseid has control over, it's likely the following 'evil Superman' are among his soldiers:

With the Crime Syndicate, the scheming Pandora and an endless army of Supermen, Darkseid has assembled the ultimate evil Justice League, leaving fans to ask how the heroes of DC's main reality can ever stand a chance against what's coming.

#3305. The 5 Most Unwatchable James Bond Movies, Ranked

The James Bond franchise has long stood as one of cinema’s most defining blockbuster titles. From the outset, way back when it started with Sean Connery in the lead role in 1962’s Dr. No, it has epitomized the suave spectacle and sophisticated charm of high-octane spy thrills. Ranging from Goldfinger to Skyfall, the saga has delivered some of the most exhilarating spy-action movies ever made, but any franchise that features 25 movies is bound to have a few misfires and, unfortunately, 007 is no different.

When the franchise is at its worst, it reduces its tropes to being crude caricatures of the genre. The gadgets become goofy, the Bond girl an affront to any form of progressive femininity, and the story often suffers most under the strain of forced stylistic choices, laughably cartoonish action sequences, and a sense of antagonism that is utterly ridiculous. Ranging from early errs that were painfully anachronistic even when they were released to more modern missteps, these blundering Bond movies represent cinema’s greatest franchise at its unwatchable worst.

Released 12 years after Connery's last Bond outing—1971’s Diamonds Are Forever—and marking just the second and latest non-Eon-produced Bond movie ever made, Never Say Never Again emerged amid a time of chaos and calamity for the franchise. Roger Moore’s ongoing tenure as the official 007 had begun to falter, and while his worst movies mark some of the franchise’s lowest points, they are made watchable through a sense of characterful campiness and, in some cases, a certain so-bad-it’s-good appeal. Neither of those attributes can be applied to Never Say Never Again, which sees a 53-year-old Connery return to the role to deliver what is effectively a tame rehash of Thunderball.

The lack of originality in the picture is only worsened by the fundamental Bond staples it was deprived of. Given it wasn’t an Eon Productions project, it never had access to the iconic Bond theme, the opening gun-barrel shot, or John Barry’s signature score. Without these qualities, the film lands with a certain flatness. It lacks authentic action-thriller energy, and its efforts to at least modernize the character by implementing ‘80s trends like arcade-style dueling only make it all the more outdated today. It isn’t the worst or most egregious Bond movie ever made, but it is among the most banal, and that pervasive sense of muted mediocrity makes it an unwatchable snoozefest in 2026.

Quantum of Solace is as bland and banal a Bond movie as has ever been made. The follow-up to Daniel Craig’s dashing debut in Casino Royale undoubtedly fell victim to the 2007/08 writer’s strike in Hollywood, making it indistinguishable from any run-of-the-mill, B-grade spy thriller. It lacks the ruthless hard-edged grunt of its predecessor, the snappy stylistic flourishes of its successor, and refuses to implement anything in the way of camp charm or thematic prowess. Even the villain’s environmental slant is ill-explored, making him an odd and forgettable concoction of timely ideals and traditional egomaniacal Bond villainy.

It is ultimately a Bond movie that lacks an identity. It doesn’t strive to be anything unique, refusing to stretch beyond the safe limitations of the franchise at its most middling and mediocre. To say it is an outright terrible film would perhaps be going too far, it just stands as a flick that has no aspiration of what it wants to be. Again, the writer’s strike of the time was definitely a limiting factor on what Quantum of Solace could achieve, but for a Bond movie to be plain boring is unforgivable. Even many of the worst installments of the franchise have their goofy eccentricities that at least give them something, but Quantum of Solace lacks anything memorable, and it derides viewers of any reason to want to rewatch it.

Most, if not all, of the original Connery Bond films have elements that haven’t aged all too well. In the best of them, it’s easily dismissed as a sign of the times, but in the lesser entries of his tenure as 007, it’s a bit more grating to watch. His fifth outing, You Only Live Twice, is the epitome of this notion. It lacks the pizzazz and pop of Connery’s earlier, more iconic movies, and it seems as though Connery himself knows it more than anyone. His performance is uncharacteristically wooden, a stilted cutout of a character where his charisma and quick-wit ought to be.

Bereft of Connery’s best work, the film struggles to apply wallpaper over the narrative cracks and biting insensitivities. Roald Dahl’s screenplay leans heavily on racial stereotypes—an idea that reaches an ugly crescendo with Bond’s infamous “yellowface” disguise as a Japanese man—and his endeavor to up the ante comes at an emotional cost. The movie is a big, drab blockbuster with no feeling, powered by senseless villainy and over-the-top theatrics. Upon release, You Only Live Once was a limp entry to the franchise, but today it is a bitterly hard-to-watch mishit that serves as a painstaking procession of every nasty trope and tendency the original Bond pictures had.

2006’s Casino Royale is a true masterpiece of action cinema, slick sophistication, and gripping high-stakes drama that finds the perfect balance between exhilarating set piece and character-charged intensity. The 1967 interpretation of the Bond story, however, is not. The unlicensed Bond adaptation follows a retired 007 (David Niven) as he is forced to re-enter the field to bring down the evil international crime faction SMERSH, which has been behind a recent series of deadly attacks on MI6 operatives. In an effort to mislead the criminal syndicate, several others also pose as agent 007, including baccarat master Evelyn Tremble (Peter Sellers) and Bond’s own former secretary, Miss Moneypenny (Barbara Bouchet).

The idea of lampooning the spy genre was good in theory, but the execution of 1967’s Casino Royale leaves much to be desired. Its story is a chaotic mess that is completely incomprehensible and never comes close to filling the film’s bloated 131-minute runtime, while on-set conflicts saw the movie pulled in several different directions, making the final product intangible. Even a supporting cast including Orson Welles, Woody Allan, and original Bond girl Ursula Andress are incapable of elevating the film beyond its pitiful nature. It was admonished by the masses upon release, and it has only gotten worse over the years.

The Bond franchise has had its fair share of mishits over the decades, but none have been quite so disastrous and agonizing as 2002’s Die Another Day. It marked an unfortunate end to Pierce Brosnan’s tenure as 007, which started out so well with GoldenEye giving a clear intent of suave style and gritty action. Three films later, the Bond saga had regressed to uninspiring uncertainty. Die Another Day is an awkward, disjointed conglomerate of the litany of Bond styles that came before it, and every tonal shift and plot twist it aspires for falls flat on its face.

The opening sequence has a certain gruffness to it, with Bond being tortured by the North Korean army over the course of 14 months, but whatever intrigue that hard-edged intro may have had immediately dissipates as the movie pivots to cringe-worthy campiness. Not only is Die Another Day’s narrative tempo off beat, its reliance on appalling CGI and ridiculous concepts to carry some of its action sequences is enough to leave viewers in hysterics. It marks an undisputed low-point for the franchise, a painful depiction of 007 at its absolute worst. The only saving grace of the movie is that it was so bad it forced producers to take an entirely new approach four years later when the saga was re-ignited with Casino Royale.

A “Captain Phillips” reunion is upon the Best Live Action Short Oscar race.

Screenwriter Billy Ray (“The Hunger Games,” “Shattered Glass,” “Richard Jewell,” Nicole Kidman’s AMC ad), who penned the 2013 Oscar-nominated “Captain Phillips, has boarded the film “Magan’s Fare” as an executive producer. The new film stars Barkhad Abdi, the Somali actor who broke out in the Paul Greengrass film and earned a Best Supporting Actor Oscar nomination.

Directed by Christopher Knoblock and Dana White, “Magan’s Fare” is vying in the Best Live Action Short race this year, having qualified out of the Raindance Film Festival where it won the top short prize. Internet Erupts Over Latest Look at Marvel Movie AI Film ‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts’ Deemed Ineligible by Academy for Best Animated Feature Oscar

The 26-minute drama stars Abdi as Magan, “a Somali-born rideshare driver who takes an older woman, Jorani (Alexis Rhee), back to her nursing home, only to discover the facility has given away her bed. With his passenger suddenly displaced and no one else willing to take responsibility for her, Magan must figure out what to do next,” per the announcement.

“The last two years have demonstrated on a grand level that small businesses need more help than big ones do,” Ray said at a recent Los Angeles screening of the film. “Well, in our community, small movies need more help than big ones do. I’m happy to be helping this small movie. I hope all of you will too. It’s so beautifully written, it’s so beautifully directed, it’s so beautifully performed. The music, the cinematography, all of it, just executed with such love and care, and integrity.”

Knoblock and White added, “We are deeply honored to have Billy Ray join our ‘Magan’s Fare’ FYC campaign as an executive producer. Billy is a remarkable storyteller whose writing creates complex, deeply human characters that stay with you long after the story ends. His work is an inspiration to us, and we’re especially excited by the opportunity to bring Billy and Barkhad Abdi back together through a film that speaks to the power of compassion and our responsibility to one another. Having Billy’s support means a great deal to us and to the heart of this film.”

#3300. Gemini app for Mac adds computer use to control desktop apps

Google is upgrading the Gemini app on Mac with computer use capabilities that can work across local desktop applications and the web.

The existing Task (previously Gemini Spark) functionality in the Mac app could just access local files in conjunction with Connected Apps, like @Gmail or @Google Calendar.

Computer use lets Gemini for Mac click and type on your behalf to accomplish multi-step tasks in local desktop apps and the web, like navigating menus and filling out forms.

Gemini works in an “isolated background window with a live preview right in your chat,” while your main screen and cursor remain free to use. On the safety front, you can stop Gemini at any time with one click, while you choose what apps Gemini uses. Google will pause for logins and payments, with confirmation needed for sensitive actions.

Many everyday tasks span desktop apps and websites that don’t connect to each other. Computer use handles the tedious steps in the background so you can save time without giving up your screen or cursor.

To use, add @Computer use to your prompt. In Customize > Connectors, you’ll see new “Desktop” apps like Blender and Autodesk Fusion join the existing Git and Obsidian integrations.

One of the best K-dramas of the year is deservedly climbing the charts on Disney+ and Hulu. Based on the 2018 web novel and later webtoon of the same name, The Remarried Empress follows titular Empress Navier (Shin Min-a), who is forced into a corner after her husband, Emperor Sovieshu (Ju Ji-hoon), throws away their marriage. The record-breaking premiere of The Remarried Empress started the series off with a bang, and the eight-episode K-drama has continually been a top performer for Disney+/Hulu since. In fact, the only title consistently outperforming it is Percy Jackson and the Olympians (via Flix Patrol).

Beyond having a built-in fandom from the hit source material, The Remarried Empress immediately attracted attention with its star-studded cast. Shin Min-a is easily one of the most renowned K-drama actresses in modern history, but pairing her with familiar heartthrob Lee Jong-suk (Heinrey) has been a true delight. Of course, there's more than enough to enjoy for viewers who aren't well-versed in the K-drama industry. Even if the basic premise doesn't instantly appeal, watching a single episode will reveal the true selling point of The Remarried Empress: a stunning, slow-burn fantasy romance that is meticulously crafted for every prospective viewer.

Despite the summary detailing major plot points like Sovieshu and Navier divorcing— and a strategic partnership with Heinrey making the latter the eponymous "remarried empress" in the first place— the Disney+ K-drama has taken an unconventional approach to adapting the illustrious webtoon. The bulk of the first season has been spent establishing its main characters and showing the audience the deterioration of Navier and Sovieshu's relationship in brutal clarity. Rather than breeze through the beginning and have Sovieshu leave the main character for Rashta (Lee Se-young) by the pilot episode's end, The Remarried Empress centers the familiar story on Navier.

Without question, each member of the extensive ensemble plays an important role in the overarching plot, but the titular character is the centerpiece of every dramatic revelation, shocking twist, and emotional decision that threatens to upend the entire empire. As the gripping narrative grows taut and tense, the stunning aesthetics of the show soften the blow, with sprawling landscapes and ornate interior shots building a beguiling setting while gorgeous costumes complement each character in their own unique color palette. Undoubtedly, the K-drama's every detail is utterly transporting, making it impossible for viewers not to fully immerse themselves in the story.

To that end, there's also incredible balance within the writing. The Remarried Empress refuses to give the audience perfect information, instead choosing deliberate moments to introduce pivotal characters, unveil transformative lore, and reveal just enough disruptive information to make the viewer question everything they know about a given subject. Consequently, The Remarried Empress wields the political drama and turmoil of a historical K-drama whilst it slowly but surely composes a love story that feels fantastic in every sense of the word. Irrefutably, the series is one of the biggest successes of the year— and it couldn't have come soon enough.

Nearly every major streaming service has invested in the production of original Korean content throughout the past decade, but Netflix K-dramas have overwhelmingly been the most popular. Be it dramas that went straight into the pop culture zeitgeist like Squid Game or multi-season favorites like All of Us Are Dead and The Trauma Code: Heroes on Call, Netflix is steadily creating K-dramas that eclipse almost anything comparable released on competing platforms. Obviously, Disney+ and Hulu have had their own successes, but titles like Moving, Made in Korea, and Perfect Crown simply don't have the same reach.

From harrowing depictions of real-life monarchies to modern twists on classic Cinderella stories, these K-dramas promise a royally good time.

As such, distributing something like The Remarried Empress— a long-awaited adaptation of a massive webtoon with a staggering cast to boot— is precisely what Disney +/Hulu needed to stay in the K-drama game. Admittedly, Netflix has dropped its fair share of amazing contributions this year, but very few can match the sheer scope of The Remarried Empress. Should the fantasy romance land a well-earned second season, Disney+ will have a multipart sensation on its hands soon enough. Yet, even if the drama isn't renewed, its eight-episode run is a worthy binge-watch that genre fans will fall head over heels for.

Don Toliver's United Kingdom show was evacuated Sunday night ... but we're told the incident wasn't as dire as some made it seem ... because tear gas was NOT involved.

Sources with direct knowledge tell TMZ ... the incident was taken out of context -- and was actually an isolated altercation in which one ticket holder used pepper spray on another, not a widespread attack on the whole audience.

Our sources say safety is still a top priority even in these isolated situations ... and -- as a matter of protocol -- the stage is being held at Co-op Live Stadium in Manchester, pending review and release, which resulted in the O2 Arena and Wembley shows being postponed.

However, Don's other remaining shows will move forward as scheduled.

As we reported ... Don was performing when a noxious substance was released on the crowd. Initial reports indicated it was tear gas -- though obviously our sources say it was just a personal pepper spray.

Emergency crews rushed to the scene -- including the Hazardous Area Response Team -- to "support the safe assessment and treatment of people at the scene."

Toliver will play at O2 and Wembley next month.

#3292. 'Blade Runner 2099' Creator Reveals the Biggest Challenge for Prime Video’s New Sci-Fi Series

In just a few days, we will be going back to the dystopian future of replicants with a new limited series from Prime Video. Blade Runner 2099 jumps the story forward 50 years and places us in a world where the replicants have finally come out on top and humans have been turned into second-class citizens. The series follows Cora (Hunter Schafer), a human who has gone undercover as a replicant, who works as a blade runner alongside Olwen (Michelle Yeoh), a dying replicant in the last days of her life.

Collider got to speak with creator and showrunner Silka Luisa and director Jonathan van Tulleken about this brand new entry into the sci-fi franchise and how the series differentiates itself from the previous two films in the universe. Van Tulleken reveals the films he drew from as reference for the visual palette of the show, and Luisa reveals the process of what it takes to transfer a story into a new format. Luisa also talks about the big change between replicants and humans and how Cora and Olwen's story gives us insight into the new dynamic between the two groups. Finally, she gives some insight into the show's connection to both Blade Runner and Blade Runner 2049 and why the show decided to lean away from drawing stronger connections to the previous film.

Going into this, what's the most daunting task when it comes to formulating the world of Blade Runner 2099?

JONATHAN VAN TULLEKEN: I think Silka had written on the page this concept of the sunshine noir, and it was beautiful because Ridley [Scott] described his movie as a 40-year-old movie set 40 years in the future. And [Jordan] Cronenweth had looked to Citizen Kane, his cinematographer, and he described Harrison Ford as a Bogart detective story. And I think, for me, when reading what Silka had written, I was going, "Well, what is our touchstone then? What is our 40 years, 40 years ago?" So I was really thinking of those movies from the 70s and 60s, you know, The French Connection by [William] Friedkin and [Alan J.] Pakula's paranoia trilogy.

What makes those films so connected to what Ridley does as well is they've so much tactility; they're based in vérité. It was where cameras were small enough that you could take them out onto the streets. I think that really led into how we wanted to approach the work, which was something that felt very human, in a way that Ridley's feels so human; it's about what it is to be human, and so we wanted to make it feel human. So we built places that were real; we used original old lights; we used the original glass from the films, the lenses. I think that allowed us to build on what Ridley started and what Denis [Villeneuve] started.

Now the replicants are the ones doing the hunting.

SILKA LUISA: I think just from the narrative perspective, obviously, there's a shift from something that is so cinematic and theatrical. It's a really different experience going into a theater and being locked in a room and letting this world wash over you. We knew we were going to be watching this on TV, and so we really had to consider what is the pace of our Blade Runner? There is a certain tempo to both films that is very meditative; I love it, it puts you in a mindset that is that world, so we were always trying to calibrate both in the writing and in the shooting and ultimately in post when we were editing, how do we pace the show?

Can you have it be this much faster heartbeat? Do you also then need to create moments of breath so that you can actually do the score, which is so iconic? Early on in editing, we had cut the episodes really, really tight just to get that propulsion of Cora's story. But we realized we really needed those breaths because without them, it's not really Blade Runner, and so we were always balancing that.

Talking about the show and the specifics of the narrative, I really like that you flip the script on what we know before, making replicants into Blade Runners who hunt humans. But how did switching the narrative of the story change the approach to how you might structure the story with the focus being on the replicants more than on humans, or at least more than in previous stories?

LUISA: Well, I think the biggest shift was that it was an undercover story. I knew because we were doing a TV show, we would have more time, and that meant that there could be a relationship at the center of the show, not just a single character and their journey. And if you want to tell a relationship story, you know, there's been so many great undercover [stories], that Donnie Brasco dynamic felt like that was going to give you a human and a replicant side-by-side, both of them hiding secrets, that would be really rich terrain.

It's interesting that in this show, you're right, you do have more room to develop things, and you have dual protagonists in the form of Cora and Olwen. Can you talk a little bit about how these two characters have a meeting of the minds as the story progresses? Because Olwen is getting older, she's dying, whereas Cora is forced to go undercover and has to be forced to think more like a replicant.

LUISA: Yeah, at the beginning of the season, both of them are really lacking empathy. Olwen because she's a replicant, and that is just something; without childhoods, they don't develop it in the same way. It's one of the defining characteristics between humans and replicants that we know from the films. And Cora is just a human who is just been stripped of her soul, because sometimes you're in these circumstances where you just are, "Go, go, go," and you can't really take a breath to even think about other people because you just are trying to live the next day. [We] wanted to tell a story of two people who really have lost this fundamental part of what the human experience is, and how can they rediscover it together? Or can they? Can a human and a replicant being side-by-side... can that awaken empathy in both of them?

I'm curious because I know this story does have connections to the original film and 2049. So considering the reveal that we get from 2049 about replicants being able to have children, I was always thinking that in the back of my mind. Why didn't you guys lean into that? Are we going to get more of that, or are there hints trickled throughout the show? Because I have thoughts.

I've seen them all, but I don't want to get too deep into spoilers, but I'm curious about your thoughts on that.

LUISA: Well, I definitely wanted to leave 2049 with enough space to tell their story, because what I love about the end of that film is it felt like it left me wanting more. I could imagine different directions for how all those characters' lives continue, and what it meant for the city, what it meant for them individually, which I think is something that Blade Runner always does. In terms of is the focus on replicants being able to have babies? No, because I feel like that is connected to the 2049 story in such a fundamental way that it felt like touching it would be making decisions for how they were to finish that film.

Blade Runner 2099 premieres November 25 on Prime Video.

#3289. Leah Remini Faces $2M Legal Fee Demand From Church of Scientology

The Church of Scientology is coming after Leah Remini ... and this time, it's hitting the former "King of Queens" star where it hurts -- her wallet.

The Church is demanding more than $2 million in attorney fees from the actress after scoring major legal victories in her ongoing lawsuit against the organization ... and it's not holding back in a blistering new statement.

According to court documents, reviewed by TMZ, the Church of Scientology International is asking a Los Angeles judge to order Remini to pay $2,044,375.39 in legal fees tied to its successful efforts to strike portions of her lawsuit ... and the Church is celebrating.

In a statement provided to TMZ Monday, Scientology claims Remini suffered a crushing defeat in her attempt to silence the organization ... arguing that trial and court rulings eliminated 90 percent of the statements she challenged.

The Church also takes aim at Remini's years of public criticism, accusing her of wanting free speech for herself while trying to deny it to Scientology.

As we previously reported ... Remini sued Scientology and its leader, David Miscavige, in 2023, alleging years of harassment, stalking and defamation after she left the Church in 2013.

While the courts have thrown out numerous allegations, her lawsuit has not been dismissed entirely ... and some claims are still moving forward.

The Church is seeking the money under California's anti-SLAPP law, which allows successful defendants to recover certain legal fees in cases involving protected speech.

A hearing on the fee request is scheduled for January ... but for now, Scientology is claiming victory ... and asking Remini to pick up a very expensive tab.

Taylor Sheridan is preparing a return to the big screen next year with his new Sicario-style action thriller, F.A.S.T., but that isn't stopping the Yellowstone writer from releasing new seasons of some of his most popular TV shows. Over the summer, it was the third season of Lioness that took the world by storm, and while the show is still in the top 10 in a handful of countries around the world, its fate beyond Season 3 has not yet been decided. Sheridan has expanded the Yellowstone universe with new shows like Dutton Ranch, the Cole Hauser and Kelly Reilly-led sequel series that aired its first season earlier this year. The show has been picked up for Season 2, but it's been confirmed that it will not make it back to streaming before the end of 2026.

However, Dutton Ranch isn't the only one of Taylor Sheridan's Yellowstone spin-offs to be thrust into the spotlight in 2026. During the first half of the year, CBS enlisted Luke Grimes to star in Marshals, the first ever network TV show set in the Yellowstone universe. It's safe to say that fans were not hot on the first season, as it registered a poor 28% on the audience-driven Popcornmeter on Rotten Tomatoes. However, Season 2, which is now in full swing and releasing new episodes every week on CBS, has begun to win fans back over. Marshals Season 2 holds a 52% on the Popcornmeter, which may not be what CBS executives are looking for, but it's still a step in the right direction after most fans agreed that the first season was one of the worst Yellowstone-adjacent projects.

The show that claimed the most of your answers is the world you were built for. If two tied, both are shown — you're complicated enough to straddle two Sheridan universes.

You are a Dutton — or you might as well be. You understand that some things are worth protecting at any cost, and that the modern world's indifference to history, to land, to legacy, is not something you're willing to accept quietly. You lead from the front, you carry your family's weight without complaint, and when someone threatens what's yours, you don't escalate — you finish it. You're not cruel. But you are absolute. In Yellowstone's world, that combination of ferocity and loyalty doesn't make you a villain. It makes you the only thing standing between everything that matters and everyone who wants to take it.

You thrive in the chaos of high-stakes negotiation, where the money is enormous, the margins are thin, and the wrong word in the wrong room can cost everyone everything. You're a fixer — the person called when a situation is already on fire and needs someone with the nerve to walk into it. West Texas oil country rewards exactly what you are: sharp, adaptable, unsentimental, and absolutely clear-eyed about what people want and what they'll do to get it. You're not naive enough to think this world is fair. You're smart enough to be the one deciding who it's fair to.

You are a Dwight Manfredi — someone who has served their time, paid their dues, and arrived somewhere unexpected with nothing but their reputation and their wits. You adapt without losing yourself. You build loyalty through respect rather than fear, though you're not above reminding people that the two aren't mutually exclusive. Tulsa King is for people who are still standing when everyone assumed they'd be finished — who find, in an unfamiliar place, that they're more capable than the world gave them credit for. You don't need a throne. You build one, wherever you happen to land.

You carry the weight of a system that is broken by design, and you do it anyway — because someone has to, and because you're the only one positioned to do it without the whole thing collapsing. Mike McLusky's world is for people who are comfortable operating where there are no good options, only less catastrophic ones. You speak every language: law enforcement, criminal, political, human. That fluency makes you invaluable and it makes you a target. You've made your peace with both. Mayor of Kingstown belongs to people who understand that keeping the peace is not the same as being at peace — and who do the job regardless.

CBS has yet to announce if Marshals has been renewed for a third season or if it will be canceled, but Kayce Dutton actor Luke Grimes is optimistic about the show's chances. As long as fans continue to watch new episodes of Marshals, CBS will likely continue to look for ways to bring the show back.

You don't need to be a programmer to get started with Anthropic's powerful AI coding tool

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you've been hearing a lot about Claude Code lately but assumed it was only for software developers, you're missing out on one of the most powerful ways to use AI right now.

Anthropic's coding agent can build websites, create personalized apps, automate repetitive tasks and develop tools that would otherwise require hours of programming experience. And thanks to the Claude desktop app, you don't even need to know how to use a terminal.

Unlike a traditional AI chatbot that gives you instructions for building something, Claude Code can do much of the work itself. You describe what you want in plain English, which is also known as "vibe coding," and Claude can create the necessary files, write the code, test its work and make adjustments based on your feedback.

Here's everything you need to know to get started, including five beginner-friendly projects worth trying.

Claude Code is Anthropic's AI coding agent. Although it was originally designed for software developers, it's also useful for anyone who wants to build their own digital tools.

Say you've been searching for a budgeting app but can't find one that does exactly what you want. Instead of downloading another app or paying for another subscription, you could ask Claude Code to build one tailored to your needs.

The biggest difference between Claude Code and a regular Claude conversation is that Claude Code can work directly with files on your computer, run commands and make changes to a project with your permission.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

You don't need to copy and paste hundreds of lines of code or figure out where to put them.

Claude Code isn't included in Anthropic's free subscription, so you'll need a paid plan to access it, with Claude Pro starting at $20 per month.

There are two main ways to get started on your computer.

Option 1: Use the Claude desktop app (recommended)

This is the easiest route for beginners because you won't have to install any additional coding software. Visit claude.com/download.

Download the app for your operating system. Install the app and sign in to your Claude account. Select the Code tab. Start a new local session and select a folder for your project. I'd recommend creating an empty folder called "My First Claude App" on your computer before getting started.

Option 2: Install Claude Code in your terminal

If you're comfortable using command-line tools, you can install Claude Code directly. On Mac or Linux, open your terminal and enter:

curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash

Once installed, enter claude and follow the instructions to authenticate your account. Anthropic also offers Claude Code through the web, where projects can run on the company's cloud infrastructure.

For your first project, I'd recommend building something small that you can actually use. A personalized daily planner is a great place to start because it doesn't require external services or complicated software.

Select your project folder and enter the following prompt:

Build me a personal daily planner that runs in my web browser. Include a to-do list, three daily priorities, a habit tracker and a notes section. Give it a clean, modern design and automatically save my progress locally. Use plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript without external dependencies. Explain how to open the finished app.

Claude should begin working on your project, creating the files necessary to make it function.

Once it's finished, ask Claude to open or preview the app. You can continue refining your creation with conversational instructions such as "Add dark mode," "Make the text bigger" or "Add a button to reset my daily tasks."

You don't have to get your initial prompt perfect. Building with Claude Code is an ongoing conversation, and some of the best features might come from ideas you have after seeing the first version.

You can create a dashboard that tracks expenses, calculates monthly savings and displays spending by category and even tailor it to your household instead of adapting to someone else's budgeting system. Try the prompt: Build me a personalized household budget tracker that runs in my web browser. Include monthly income, recurring bills, everyday expenses and savings goals. Automatically calculate how much money I have left each month and display spending by category using interactive charts. Let me add, edit and delete expenses, customize spending categories and track my progress toward savings goals. Give it a clean, modern design and save my data locally so it stays private. Explain how to open and use the finished app.

Build a personal portfolio, small-business website or blog. Describe the colors, layout and features you want, then refine the design as you go.

Try the prompt: Build me a professional personal portfolio website with a clean, modern design, a warm color palette and easy navigation. Include a homepage, an About Me section, a gallery of my work and a contact page. Make it mobile-friendly and easy to update. Use placeholder text and images that I can replace with my own content. Explain how to preview the website and publish it online when I'm ready.

Create a weekly dinner planner that generates a shopping list based on your selections. You could even add a feature that rotates your family's favorite meals.

Try the prompt: Build me a weekly meal-planning app that lets me plan dinners from Monday through Sunday and automatically generates a grocery shopping list based on my selections. Include a recipe library where I can save my family's favorite meals, customize serving sizes and rotate meals to avoid repetition. Organize the shopping list by grocery store department and let me check off items as I shop. Give it a clean, colorful, mobile-friendly design and save my meal plans locally. Explain how to open and use the finished app.

Ask Claude to develop a tool that identifies duplicate files, categorizes downloads or renames photos. Start with copies of your files and ask Claude to preview its proposed changes.

Try this prompt: Build me a file organization tool that identifies duplicate files, sorts downloads into folders by file type and renames photos by date. Start with a test folder containing copies of my files. Preview all proposed changes and ask for my approval before moving, renaming or deleting anything.

From personalized trivia games to interactive math quizzes for your kids, Claude Code can help you create something entertaining without downloading a game development platform.Try this prompt: Build me an interactive trivia game that runs in my web browser. Include customizable categories such as animals, science, movies and math, with three difficulty levels suitable for kids and adults. Give players multiple-choice questions, immediate feedback, a running score and fun animations for correct answers. Include a multiplayer mode so family members can compete against each other. Make the design colorful, mobile-friendly and easy to navigate. Let me add my own trivia questions and explain how to open and play the finished game.

Start with Plan Mode. Claude Code can outline its approach before modifying your project. This gives you an opportunity to review what it's proposing and make adjustments before it starts building.

Be careful with permissions. Claude Code can modify files and execute commands. I recommend using manual approval settings when you're getting started. Never authorize an action you don't understand, and keep backups of important files.

Ask Claude to test its work. Once your project is finished, ask Claude to check for errors, test every button and make sure everything functions as expected. AI-generated software can contain bugs, even when it looks polished.

What makes Claude Code a lot of fun is that you can simply explain what you want and it will create it. Even if you've never coded at all or have no idea what writing code even looks like, you can build your own software. Just start slow and think about a small frustration in your everyday life that an app or website might be able to fix. You might be surprised by what you can build with a few well-written prompts.

#3283. Six Things You Should Do Now to Optimize Your Setup for GTA 6

You’re almost ready for Grand Theft Auto VI. You’ve preloaded the game on your console, you’ve taken the next month off work, and you’ve locked your phone in a Faraday cage and set it adrift at sea. You’re prepared to lock in, and you haven’t forgotten a thing…right? Well, just to make sure, here are the most important tips to optimize your setup before you fire up the most anticipated game of the decade.

GTA 6 is absurdly large. According to Rockstar, you’ll need up to 212GB of storage space. For high-end consoles like the PS5 Pro, that’s more than 10% of the available storage space, and close to half the space on the more budget-conscious Xbox Series S. There’s a good chance you’ll have to delete something to make room.

Alternatively, it’s pretty easy to add more storage (if you can afford it). External SSDs are probably the cheapest route, though you’ll want to make sure to use a high-speed USB cable to connect it. It’s even worth shopping around for alternate models of SSD. For example, at the time of writing, the popular 2TB WD_BLACK external drive was close to $200, but the exact same drive in pink was $132.

You can also directly upgrade the storage of your console with expansion drives. The Xbox Series X|S supports proprietary expansion cards, while the PS5 and PS5 Pro can accept most M.2 internal SSDs. These will generally be faster, since they plug directly into the console via higher-speed connections than a drive hooked up via USB.

Let’s face it: Half the fun of any sandbox game is the weird, unique stuff that happens to only you. So you’re probably going to be hitting that “record recent gameplay” button more often than usual. While you’re cleaning up your storage space (or adding more), make sure to account for all the video clips you might want to save.

File size of video clips depends on a lot of factors, but 4K recordings can generally take up to 0.5GB per minute of footage. You can cut that down by saving footage in 1080p instead, but either way you’ll want to leave a little extra space.

Game footage is also a pretty good place to look if you need to make room on your console and don’t want to delete any games. Be honest with yourself: You don’t need all those clips from Horizon Forbidden West you saved four years ago. Dive into the settings on your console and find the biggest media files you forgot you even had on there.

According to Rockstar, GTA 6 will be targeting 30fps across consoles at launch, which is pretty low as modern AAA games go. Part of the reason for that is all the processing power going to rendering a complex environment, but it also means you won’t need a fancy high frame rate TV or monitor any time soon to get the most out of it. Still, it couldn’t hurt to check a few settings on your display.

First, make sure you’re using a higher refresh rate than 30Hz. While the game is targeting 30fps, it is technically capable of more, so if your console can keep up, you don’t want to accidentally bottleneck your frames. This setting will vary by device, so check the manual that came with your screen.

Also, make sure you have HDR enabled on your hardware. There’s a good chance this is already turned on for your TV, but sometimes other devices can switch display modes if they only support SDR. The game will help you calibrate your HDR settings for GTA 6 specifically when you launch it, but only if it detects HDR compatibility in the first place.

If you’re planning to buy a console specifically for GTA 6, this might be one of those rare instances where a PS5 Pro really is worth the upgrade. According to Rockstar, certain features like ray-traced shadows will only be available on the Pro version of Sony’s console.

More importantly, the PS5 Pro version supports PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (or PSSR), which upscales lower-resolution images to get better detail and higher frame rates out of the same hardware. Given that GTA 6 is already starting at a meager target of 30fps on most consoles, anything that can give your frame rate a boost is probably going to feel like a welcome improvement over the baseline.

I’ll tell you a secret as someone who’s spent a lot of time testing different game controllers: Most of the time, you really don’t need an expensive “elite” controller. Most of the time. I don’t buy into the idea that a taller control stick is going to make you an esports athlete. It can be nice to have, but it’s not a game changer. What does matter is customizing your controls, especially for long gaming sessions.

The DualSense Edge wireless controller is a favorite of mine, mainly because of the rear paddles and adjustable triggers. The former lets you map any button to a rear lever that you can access with your fingers underneath the controller, which can often ease some of the wrist strain of awkward button combos. And the adjustable triggers let you activate the buttons with less motion, again reducing repetitive stress.

The Xbox Elite Series 2 controller has similar features for the Xbox, as well as custom caps for the D-pad. Both consoles’ versions of pro controllers are more expensive than the standard ones, but if you’re planning to game for many hours, it can be worth it to get a controller that’s more comfortable for you.

If you have an Xbox One, you don’t necessarily have to upgrade your console to play GTA 6, but you might want to take a look at your network. GTA 6 will be available on Xbox Cloud Gaming on day one, and you’ll be able to stream the game to an Xbox One console (as long as you purchase Cloud playtime as well or get some with your Game Pass subscription). This is the only way to play on a console older than the current generation, so if you don’t want to shell out for new hardware, this might be your best bet.

Xbox recommends a minimum of a 20Mbps connection to run cloud gaming, but more is obviously better. If you can connect your console to a wired Ethernet connection, that would be better and provide more stability. If you can’t connect a cable, then at least make sure you’re well within range of your wifi router, and try to limit any other bandwidth-hogging applications on the network while you’re playing.

#3281. Apple fires back at Epic over claims it withheld 122,000 documents

Apple has responded to Epic Games’ filing from last Friday, pushing back against accusations that it improperly withheld more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions. Here are the details.

While the Supreme Court is set to review whether the civil contempt designation against Apple should be upheld in its lawsuit against Epic Games, the two companies have also been battling in the district court over what commission, if any, Apple should be allowed to charge on purchases made through external payment systems.

Apple submitted its proposal to the district court on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, but Epic is disputing not just the basis for those proposed rates, but also Apple’s handling of document production in the proceedings.

As part of the proceedings, Epic had submitted 16 categories of documents it wanted Apple to produce (including “internal analyses of the financial or business impact” of its proposed commissions and “communications relating to any strategies to dissuade developers from offering link-outs”), along with a list of current and former Apple employees whose records should be searched.

Apple agreed to use Epic’s proposed search terms and include all employees, and began producing documents it determined were responsive to Epic’s requests.

Epic, however, said last Friday that Apple was improperly withholding more than 122,000 documents matching those search terms from the records of the seven initial employees, and asked the court to order Apple to produce all matching non-privileged documents, regardless of its relevance assessments.

Which brings us to Apple’s newest filing.

In its filing, Apple argues that contrary to Epic’s claim that its proposed search terms were “tailored” to the proceedings over link-out fees, they were actually “overbroad,” capturing large numbers of unrelated documents.

For instance, Apple notes that while intended to identify documents related to its proposed commission rates, Epic’s “commission*” search term also “captures documents that refer to government and private commissions, as well as documents hitting on the totally irrelevant term ‘commissioner,’ such as documents discussing the NFL Commissioner.”

“[…] the use of a wildcard in a search string is designated by the asterisk symbol, which means that the search string will hit on any term that includes the prefix before the asterisk.

In the same vein, Apple notes that “Epic’s use of ‘fee*’ in its search strings related to litigation and Apple’s link-out-related projects pulled in documents containing words like ‘feel,’ ‘feed,’ ‘feedback,’ ‘feet,’ and ‘feeble’ without the word ‘fee’ or ‘fees’ appearing at all.”

Apple’s overall argument is that these unrelated matches account for the vast majority of documents identified by Epic’s searches, and it cites legal precedent to argue that it should only be required to produce documents responsive to Epic’s requests, rather than every document matching the agreed-upon search terms:

In fact, at least 95% of the Initial Custodian Document Population hit on generic terms like these and did not include any reference to the term “link-out” or its variations, despite that concept being central to the Proffer and related discovery. These sweeping terms do not just increase the total volume of the Initial Custodian Document Population, they also captured highly sensitive and irrelevant documents, such as Apple employees’ personal tax or financial records, medical records, documents discussing unannounced products, documents containing passwords, investor-relations materials, and privileged or protected legal communications.

The law is clear: parties are only required to produce responsive documents, not every document returned by a search string. […] (“The Court will not compel defendants to produce any document simply because it contains a search term whether or not it is responsive to the discovery request.”). Epic has not shown, and cannot show, why the regular discovery process should be disrupted here. Speculation based on hit counts, particularly where the producing party can explain low responsiveness rates, does not justify the extraordinary and unprecedented remedy Epic seeks.

Apple goes on to argue that complying with Epic’s demands would require extensive additional work, including reviewing documents for privileged or sensitive information and redacting protected material, making it impossible to meet Epic’s proposed December 2 deadline.

Finally, Apple asks the court to reject Epic’s motion but proposes that, should the court decide that some intervention is warranted, a randomized, statistically significant sample of the documents it deems nonresponsive be submitted to a Special Master for independent review, rather than producing all of them to Epic directly.

Fjord follows the Gheorghius, a Romanian-Catholic family who move to a remote Norwegian village hoping to build a quieter life. As they grow close to their neighbors, the Halbergs, cultural differences and local suspicion begin to turn that welcome into hostility, leading to accusations that threaten both families and expose the fragile line between trust and fear.

#3278. You Can Get One of These Pocket E-Readers for As Little As $55 Before Black Friday

Black Friday is usually a great time to grab a new e-reader, but the ongoing RAM crisis has made that a question mark this year: Amazon recently raised the prices of all its Kindles by around $50 and refreshed the entire lineup, which means your odds of grabbing one at a big discount are low. But you aren't totally out of luck: If you haven't noticed, micro-e-readers—I'm talking credit card-sized, with screens that measure around four inches—are all the rage in 2026, and right now, you can pick up one of them for around $55.

If you too can see the appeal of carrying all of your books with you on a device so small you'll forget it's even in your pocket, it's a great time to jump in: The recently released Xteink X4 Classic is currently 38% off for Black Friday, bringing it down to $54.87, a record-low price. Meanwhile, the smaller X3 is $55.72, or 19% off. Both are available in either "mist grey" or "space black." The discounts should last through the end of Cyber Monday on Nov. 30.

Xteink is a Chinese startup that shook up the e-reading world last year with the launch of the X4, a super bare-bones device that made up for its lack of features and usability with a cheap sub-$70 price point. Since then, a huge online community of fans has formed, sharing tips on Reddit and even coming together to crowdsource an alternate operating system that fixed a lot of early problems. Xteink quickly followed up the X4 with a slate of other devices, including the 3.7-inch X3 and the X4 Pro, which adds a front light and touchscreen (at the cost of screen clarity and two physical buttons).

The X4 Classic and the X3 improve on the original X4 with quality-of-life upgrades like a larger battery, relocated page-turn buttons, a real-time clock, and a tilt-to-turn-page feature. They're also lighter and thinner than the X4, though there is a trade-off involved: They drop the USB-C charging port in favor of magnetic pogo pins that require a separate adapter (included).

These upgrades also increased the cost: The X4 Classic typically retails for $89, $20 more than the discontinued X4 and only $10 less than the X4 Pro, while the X3 launched at $79. But right now, the X4 Classic is just under $55, or around 38% off, and the X3 is about a dollar more. Either is a great option for those who prioritize crisp, readable text above the conveniences of a built-in light or touchscreen, as those add extra layers between the inner screen and outer glass. It's also important to understand what you're getting into: These devices support only e-books without Digital Rights Management (DRM), which means you can't use it to read your existing library of Kindle books. On the plus side, there's no longer a need to worry about flashing new firmware if you don't want to, as the native version has been totally overhauled and is now one of your best options (though the new firmware, called "Licorice," isn't available on the X3 quite yet).

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

No. If you find the product you're looking for with a major discount right now, get it. It's not likely to drop any lower, but it could always run out of stock. Take advantage of price matching or guarantees instead of waiting. Remember, you can always return products later if you change your mind. For the majority of products, the deal from Black Friday will be the same one on Cyber Monday.

It blows my mind that there are people out there who choose to go naked with their phones. Between the smooth casing and the constant threat of accidentally dropping my iPhone 18 Pro, going naked gives me way too much anxiety — so I honestly could never bring myself to do it.

That’s why the PhoneBack by Süti immediately caught my eye. Rather than wrapping my iPhone 18 Pro in a silicone or polycarbonate shell that adds bulks to its size, it’s a minimalist magnetic backplate that protects the rear — while also sprinkling a little of style at the same time. For someone like me who refuses to go caseless, it’s easily the closest alternative I’d be willing to go to achieve that naked iPhone look. Here’s why.

Do you hate bulky cases? Well, the Süti PhoneBack is one of the easiest, most efforless iPhone cases around since it snaps onto the back via MagSafe to protect the back glass and camera bump. At just 2.34 mm thin, it adds welcome grip and lets you swap styles, all without adhesives or blocking wireless charging.

What I really love about the PhoneBack is how clever it is at delivering just enough protection against everyday wear and tear, all while completely preserving the "naked" look and feel of the iPhone 18 Pro. Since it relies on a MagSafe connection, it takes seconds to snap directly onto the back — and it beats having to deal with the headaches of installing one of those adhesive vinyl skins.

Best of all, the PhoneBack by Süti gives me a quick and effortless way to change the colors or textures whenever the mood strikes, unlike a permanent wrap that’s notoriously difficult to peel off.

Options range from soft-touch Silicone that I feel is more scratch-resistant, the two-tone look of the iCandy cases, to my favorite NanoLeather one that adds texture to the back of my iPhone 18 Pro. One of the downsides of upgrading from the iPhone 17 Pro to the 18 Pro is that the former’s signature Cosmic Orange color isn’t available, but I’m able to easily emulate that look with the orange silicone PhoneBack.

Even though the Süti PhoneBack uses magnets to snap onto my iPhone, it doesn't get in the way of wireless charging at all. That’s because it packs a neodymium magnet array, which still lets me drop the phone right onto a MagSafe or Qi2 charging pad without ever pulling the backplate off. On top of that, I can keep using my favorite MagSafe accessories — like magnetic wallets, desk stands, car mounts, power banks, and more.

I’ll say it again: the Süti PhoneBack is hands down the closest I’ll ever get to rocking a naked iPhone 18 Pro. It strikes that balance I want with its minimalist design, extra grip, and effortless customization — all without sacrificing MagSafe charging or accessory support. That said, I still have to be very careful because it leaves the sides and front glass completely exposed. If you want full 360-degree drop protection, stick with a traditional case. But if you crave that bare-metal feel in hand and just want scratch protection and a fresh look for the back, the PhoneBack is tough to beat.

He's enjoying plenty of success on streaming at the moment with the likes of MobLand, The Gentlemen, and Young Sherlock, but some of his older movies have also found an audience that wasn't necessarily there when they were released in theaters as a result of Ritchie's big wins on the small screen. A decade ago, Ritchie decided to try his hand at a $175 million fantasy epic that Warner Bros. had hoped would launch an entire franchise, but those plans were abandoned when the movie failed to make back its production budget at the box office. Nine years later, though, it's becoming one of those Netflix sleeper hits.

Ritchie's King Arthur: Legend of the Sword has officially recorded 179 million minutes viewed on Netflix, placing eighth on Nielsen's movie streaming chart in the United States for the week of November 2–8. Given the movie's 126-minute runtime, that's the equivalent of approximately 1.42 million complete viewings in a single week.

The film is an iconoclastic take on the classic Excalibur myth, tracing Arthur's journey from the streets to the throne. When the child Arthur's father is murdered, Vortigern, Arthur's uncle, seizes the crown. Robbed of his birthright and with no idea who he truly is, Arthur comes up the hard way in the back alleys of the city. But once he pulls the sword from the stone, his life is turned upside down and he is forced to acknowledge his true legacy — whether he likes it or not.

King Arthur: Legend of the Sword grossed just $149.2 million worldwide against its $175 million production budget, which obviously isn't the result anybody was hoping for. Critically, it didn't fare much better either, sitting on a 31% critics' score on Rotten Tomatoes. However, at least the audience kinda liked it, as it has a considerably healthier 69% audience score. Nice.

The cast includes Charlie Hunnam (Sons of Anarchy) as Arthur, Jude Law (The Holiday) as Vortigern, Àstrid Bergès-Frisbey (Pirates of the Caribbean: On Stranger Tides) as the Mage, Djimon Hounsou (Gladiator) as Bedivere, Eric Bana (Troy) as Uther Pendragon, Aidan Gillen (Game of Thrones) as Bill, Freddie Fox (House of the Dragon) as Rubio, and Annabelle Wallis (Peaky Blinders) as Maggie.

King Arthur: Legend of the Sword is streaming now on Netflix in the United States. Stay tuned to Collider for all the latest news and updates on the biggest and best movies and shows heading to your favorite streaming platforms soon.

#3273. Next year’s iPhone Pro redesign sounds like exactly what I’ve been wanting

Rumors about next year’s 20th anniversary iPhone Pro models have been ramping up, and they suggest Apple is designing an ‘iPhone 20 Pro’ that combines traits from two current models.

Apple keeps expanding the iPhone line to include new models. And while it’s great that there are more models for differing preferences and needs, it’s also left me missing the days of having one model that was the clear “best.”

That problem isn’t going away, since the iPhone Duo represents a brand new type of iPhone that some users will love, while others find it isn’t for them.

With my failed iPhone Duo experiment over, I’m back to using iPhone 18 Pro as my default model. But I still have an iPhone Air around for work, and every time I pick it up, I’m struck by how impressive it remains.

I used the iPhone Air all of last year and loved it. The main reason I upgraded to an iPhone 18 Pro is the camera system. I have young children at home—including newborn twins—and want to capture the best possible photos before they get older.

iPhone 18 Pro’s Main camera has been fantastic, and it’s great having the Telephoto again too.

But I still sorely miss the overall design of the iPhone Air. And it sounds like next year, I could get the best of both models.

Rumors indicate Apple’s 20th anniversary iPhone Pro models will have a unique new design featuring a quad-curved display that makes it look bezel-free.

The new models are expected to also be a bit slimmer, use curved edges, and possibly even bring back titanium. Leakers say the new design borrows a lot from the iPhone Air’s look.

This sounds like exactly what I’ve been hoping for.

If they make one the size of the iPhone 13 mini I will buy. Otherwise I'm holding out

While the ‘iPhone 20 Pro’ certainly won’t—and shouldn’t—be as thin as iPhone Air, if it can slim down a little and adopt several other Air design traits, I suspect it will evoke the same affection the Air has.

But unlike the Air, the new Pro model will still offer the best camera system in an iPhone (not to mention better battery life).

As a huge fan of the design of the Air, and the functionality of the 18 Pro, Apple’s 20th anniversary iPhone model could prove the perfect model for me. And for anyone else not opting for iPhone Duo 2.

What do you think of the rumored iPhone 20 Pro design? Let us know in the comments.
